simple-drawings.title: Simple Drawings
simple-drawings.blurb: The SIFT's opening speed test: five tiny line drawings, four identical and one different. Learn how it's scored, the pace that pays and a scan that finds the odd one in four looks or fewer.

units.title: How the test works
units.objective: Know the format, the clock and how your score is counted.

steps: Each item shows five small line drawings, A to E. Four are exactly the same and one is different. Tap the different one.
The real SIFT gives you about 100 items in 2 minutes, just over a second each. Nobody is expected to finish. The app's drill uses the same 2-minute clock.
The difference is always exactly one line: a line added, a line taken away, or one line changed (drawn to a different spot). Everything else, including any dot, is identical.
Wrong answers cost you. The app scores you as right answers minus a quarter of your wrong answers, so a careless tap undoes part of a good one.
That penalty is set so blind guessing earns nothing on average. Your score comes from quick, honest spotting, not from fast tapping.
teach.formula: corrected score = right − (wrong ÷ 4)

worked.stem: In a 2-minute drill you answer 60 items: 52 right and 8 wrong. What is your corrected score?
steps: Penalty: wrong ÷ 4 = 8 ÷ 4 = 2.
Corrected score: right − penalty = 52 − 2.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Look at the five pictures in a row.
Four of them are twins: every line is in the same place.
One is not a twin. Something about its lines is different.
Tap that one. That is the whole job.
Each right tap is +1 point. Each wrong tap takes away a quarter of a point.
So go quickly, but only tap once you have actually seen the difference.

practice.stem: Which drawing is different from the other four?
practice.explain: C is different: it has a fourth line closing the left side, which makes a full box. The other four are open on the left.

practice.stem: On the real SIFT, Simple Drawings gives you about —
practice.explain: About 100 items in 2 minutes, a little over a second each. 50 in 5 minutes is Hidden Figures, and 25 in 10 minutes is Spatial Apperception.

practice.stem: You finish a drill with 40 right and 12 wrong. Using right − (wrong ÷ 4), what is your corrected score?
practice.explain: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, and 40 − 3 = 37. Those 12 careless taps cost you 3 whole points.

practice.stem: Which drawing is different from the other four?
practice.explain: E is missing the short flat line along the bottom. The other four all have it.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Think of it as a spot-the-difference game against the clock.
steps: It's spot the difference, but with five pictures instead of two.
Four of the pictures are photocopies of each other. One is not.
The change is always one line: one extra, one missing, or one drawn in a different place.
There are about 100 items in 2 minutes, so you won't finish. That is normal for everyone.
Right answers add 1. Wrong answers take off ¼. So tap as soon as you have seen the difference, and not before.

units.title: Speed, accuracy and the guessing penalty
units.objective: Find the pace that scores the most once wrong answers are taken off.

steps: Your score isn't how many items you tap. It is right answers minus a quarter of your wrong ones.
A blind tap hits the odd drawing 1 time in 5. Over five blind taps you gain +1 for the hit and lose ¼ four times for the misses: 0 overall. Blind guessing earns nothing and burns time.
If you can rule out even one drawing, a quick pick from the rest is worth a little more than nothing. Narrow it to two and a pick is clearly worth taking.
Most errors come from tapping before you have seen the difference, not from hard items. One honest look per item keeps accuracy high.
Aim for a steady rhythm of about one item a second with very few misses. Extra speed only helps while your accuracy stays high.

worked.stem: Ana attempts 70 items: 50 right, 20 wrong. Ben attempts 55: 54 right, 1 wrong. Who has the higher corrected score?
steps: Ben tapped fewer items but got almost all of them right.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture a jar of coins. Every right tap drops in one whole coin.
Every wrong tap takes out a quarter of a coin.
If you tap without looking, you are right about 1 time in 5.
Five blind taps: 1 coin in, 4 quarters out. The jar is back where it started.
So blind tapping is wasted time.
Looking for about a second, then tapping, is what fills the jar.

practice.stem: In the app's scoring, each wrong answer —
options: takes away a quarter of a point
practice.explain: Corrected score = right − (wrong ÷ 4), so each wrong answer takes away a quarter of a point.

practice.stem: If you tap one of the five drawings without looking, on average that tap adds —
practice.explain: 1 time in 5 you gain 1; 4 times in 5 you lose ¼. 1/5 − 4/5 × 1/4 = 1/5 − 1/5 = 0. It adds nothing and costs time.

practice.stem: Kai attempts 80 items: 56 right, 24 wrong. Lee attempts 62: 60 right, 2 wrong. Who has the higher corrected score?
options: You can't tell without the time
practice.explain: Kai: 56 − 24 ÷ 4 = 56 − 6 = 50. Lee: 60 − 2 ÷ 4 = 59.5. Lee wins by staying accurate, even though Kai attempted more.

practice.stem: You have ruled out two drawings and can't choose between the other three. What is a quick pick from those three worth on average?
practice.explain: A 1/3 chance of +1 and a 2/3 chance of −1/4: 1/3 − 2/12 = 1/3 − 1/6 = +1/6. Small but positive, so make the pick and move on rather than stall.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's look at it like a deal: what does each tap buy you?
steps: A right tap buys you 1 point. A wrong tap costs you a quarter of a point.
A blind tap is right only 1 time in 5. That is 1 point gained and 4 quarters lost: you break even.
Breaking even while burning time is a bad deal. You could have spent that second on an item you can actually see.
Rule out one drawing and the deal tips in your favour. Rule out three and it is a good deal.
So the best plan is a steady pace with honest looks: fast, but never blind.

example.stem: Sam attempts 90: 60 right, 30 wrong. Jo attempts 70: 68 right, 2 wrong. Who scores higher?
steps: Jo wins by about 15 points while attempting fewer.

reteach.hook: Blind taps break even. Honest looks win.

check.stem: You can rule out three drawings and you're stuck between two. A quick pick between them is worth, on average —
check.explain: 1/2 × 1 − 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/2 − 1/8 = 3/8 of a point. That pick is worth taking.

check.stem: Max attempts 100: 70 right, 30 wrong. Ria attempts 75: 74 right, 1 wrong. Who has the higher corrected score?
check.explain: Max: 70 − 7.5 = 62.5. Ria: 74 − 0.25 = 73.75. Accuracy beats volume.

check.stem: Most Simple Drawings mistakes come from —
options: tapping before you've actually seen the difference
items that are too hard to solve
check.explain: The items are simple; errors mostly come from rushing the tap. One honest look per item keeps accuracy high.

check.stem: Which drawing is different from the other four?
check.explain: C is different: the lower left line ends one dot further right, so it crosses the lower right line instead of meeting it in a point at the bottom. The other four meet in one bottom point.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it up one step at a time.
steps: Each right answer: +1 point.
Each wrong answer: −¼ point.
If you tap without looking, you will usually be wrong.
Out of 5 blind taps, about 1 is right and 4 are wrong.
1 right = +1. 4 wrong = −¼ four times = −1.
+1 and −1 make 0. Blind taps get you nothing.
So look first. Then tap.

example.stem: You tap 5 times without looking: 1 right, 4 wrong. How many points did you gain?
steps: The 1 right tap gives +1.
The 4 wrong taps give −¼ each, which is −1.

reteach.hook: Look, then tap. Never tap blind.

check.stem: How much does one wrong answer take away?
check.explain: Each wrong answer takes away a quarter of a point.

check.stem: Four wrong answers take away —
check.explain: 4 × ¼ = 1 point.

check.stem: What should you do before you tap?
check.explain: Look first, then tap. That keeps your wrong answers low.

check.stem: Which drawing is different from the other four?
check.explain: D has an extra flat line across the top. The other four don't.

units.title: Scanning: compare to the majority
units.objective: Find the odd drawing in four looks or fewer, and know the usual differences.

steps: Don't compare every drawing with every other one: that is 10 pairs. Find the majority pattern and check each drawing against it.
Look at A and B. If they match, that is the pattern. Check C, D and E against it; the one that breaks it is the answer.
If A and B differ, one of them is the odd one. Check C: whichever of A or B matches C is normal, so the other one is the answer.
When checking, run one feature along the row at a time: the number of lines, the longest line, the slants, where the lines end. One feature is faster than the whole picture.

There are only three kinds of difference: an extra line, a missing line, or one line changed. Count the lines first; one more or one fewer gives the answer at a glance. If every drawing has the same count, one line has changed, so compare angles and end points.
teach.formula: A = B → check C, D, E against A.   A ≠ B → whichever matches C is normal.

worked.stem: A and B are different. C looks exactly like B. Which drawing is the odd one?
steps: Only one drawing is different, so A and B can't both be normal.
C matches B, so B's pattern is the majority.
A doesn't match it, so A is the odd one. D and E don't need checking.
worked.answer: A

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of five soldiers in a line. Four wear the same uniform.
Look at the first two. Same uniform? Then that is the standard uniform.
Walk down the line and find the soldier who doesn't match it.
First two different? Look at the third soldier. Whoever matches the third is in standard uniform.
The one left over is the odd one.
You never need to compare every soldier with every other soldier.

practice.stem: A and B look identical. What is the fastest next step?
options: Compare C with D, then D with E
Check C, D and E against A
practice.explain: Two matching drawings show you the majority pattern. Now just check the other three against it.

practice.stem: Which drawing is different from the other four?
practice.explain: C is different: its slanted line runs down to the right from the upright line instead of up to the right. Every drawing has three lines, so the count can't help here; one line has changed.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's find the 'normal' drawing first, then hunt for the one that isn't.
steps: Before you hunt for the odd drawing, find a normal one. Two matching drawings are always normal.
A and B match? Then A is normal. Hold A in your head and glance at C, D and E.
A and B don't match? One of them is odd. Glance at C: the one of A or B that matches C is normal.
Check one feature at a time: count the lines, then look at the slants, then where each line ends.
One more or one fewer line shows up in the count. Same count everywhere? Then one line has changed: look for a different angle or end point.

steps: Only one drawing is odd.
D doesn't match the normal pattern, so D is the odd one.
E must be normal, so you can tap D straight away.

options: one line in a different place

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One small step on each screen.
steps: Look at the first picture, A.
Look at the second picture, B.
Are A and B the same? If yes, they show what 'normal' looks like.
Now look at C. Same as A? Then it's normal too.
Keep going along the row.
The first picture that doesn't match A is your answer.
If A and B were different, look at C. The one C matches is normal; the other is your answer.

hidden-figures.title: Hidden Figures
hidden-figures.blurb: Find which of five shapes is hidden in a busy drawing, at the same size and the same way up. Learn the shapes, the anchor-corner search and how to reject the decoys.

units.title: The shapes: exact size, exact way up
units.objective: Learn the reference shapes and what counts as a true copy.

steps: First you see five reference shapes, labelled A to E. Every drawing that follows hides exactly one of them.
In the app, each run uses five of eight shapes: square, L-shape, cross, house, cut-corner square, diamond, chevron and triangle. Spend your first seconds learning the five you've got.
The hidden copy is exactly the same size and the same way up as the reference. It is never turned, flipped, stretched or shrunk.
So an L turned on its side, or a triangle pointing the other way, is NOT a match, even though it is 'the same kind of shape'.
In the app every shape fills the same size of box, and every line runs flat, upright or at 45°. Use that box size as your ruler.
The real SIFT gives 50 items in 5 minutes, about 6 seconds each, and wrong answers are penalised.

worked.stem: The reference is an L-shape: a narrow stem on the left and a foot running right along the bottom. In a drawing you find an L whose foot runs LEFT. Is that the hidden figure?
steps: Its foot runs the other way, so it is a mirror image of the reference.
Hidden copies are never flipped or turned.
It is not a match. Keep looking for an L with the foot running right, at the same size.
worked.answer: No: a mirrored L is not a match

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of a cookie cutter.
The hidden shape was pressed into the drawing with that exact cutter.
Same cutter means same size: not bigger, not smaller.
The cutter is never turned or flipped over before it is pressed.
So you are hunting for an exact copy, sitting the same way up as the reference.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's think of the hidden shape as a stamp pressed into the drawing.
steps: A rubber stamp always prints the same picture at the same size.
The hidden shape is a stamp print: exactly the reference, at exactly its size.
Nobody turned the stamp before pressing it, so the print is the same way up as the reference.
So a turned, mirrored, bigger or smaller version is not the print. It's a different stamp.
Pick a corner of the reference (for a triangle, where its square corner is) and make sure the copy has it in the same place.

units.title: The anchor-corner search
units.objective: Find a hidden shape fast by hunting for its most distinctive corner first.

steps: Don't try to see a whole outline at once in the clutter. Pick one feature only that shape has: its anchor.

Good anchors: the house's pointed roof, the cut-corner square's one sloped corner, the chevron's downward V, the cross's four inside corners, the L's inside corner where stem meets foot, the triangle's long slope, the diamond's points.
Scan the drawing for that anchor. Every place it appears is a candidate.
From the anchor, trace the outline: does each edge run the right length, turn the right way and close up?
Then check the inside. The real hidden figure has a clean inside: no line crosses through it.
Plain shapes like the square have weak anchors, so test the distinctive shapes first and come back to the plain ones.

worked.stem: The five shapes are A L-shape, B square, C house, D triangle, E chevron. The green outline in the picture shows where the hidden one sits. How does the anchor search find it?
steps: Start with the most distinctive anchor. For the house, that is a pointed roof: two 45° lines meeting at a peak, on top of two short upright walls.
Scan for it: it appears in the centre.
Trace out from the anchor: every edge is there, at the right length and the same way up as the reference.
Check the inside: no line crosses it. The other outlines in the drawing (triangle, L-shape, square) each have a line running through them.
worked.answer: C, the house

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of looking for a friend in a crowd. You don't study every face; you look for their bright red hat.
Each shape has its own 'red hat': one corner or point that the other shapes don't have.
For the house, it is the pointed roof. For the L, the one inside corner.
Look for the red hat first. When you find it, check the rest of the shape around it.
If the whole outline is there and nothing crosses its inside, you've found it.

practice.stem: Which is the best anchor to hunt for when the shape is the house?

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's treat each shape like a person with one stand-out feature.
steps: If you're meeting someone off a train, you look for the one thing that marks them out, like a red hat.
Each shape's red hat is its anchor: house = pointed roof, chevron = downward V, cross = four inside corners, L = one inside corner.
Triangle = long 45° slope down to the right. Cut-corner square = one sloped corner at the top right. Diamond = four points.
Sweep the drawing looking only for that anchor. Ignore everything else.
When you find it, trace the rest of the outline, then check the inside is clean.

example.stem: You're hunting for the cross. What do you scan the drawing for first?
steps: Flat and upright lines are everywhere, so they won't help.
The cross is the only shape with four inside corners close together around a middle square.
Scan for that cluster of inside corners, then trace the arms.

reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One small step at a time.
steps: Look at one reference shape.
Find the one corner or point that makes it special.
For the house, that's the pointed roof.
Now look in the drawing for that special corner.
When you find it, look at the lines around it.
Do they make the whole shape? Is the inside empty?
If yes, you've found the hidden shape.

units.title: Rejecting the near-misses
units.objective: Tell the true hidden figure from decoys that almost match.

steps: Every drawing holds decoys: outlines that look like the other options but aren't clean copies.
In the app, two or three of the other option shapes are drawn complete, but with a straight line running through the middle. A line through the inside rules a shape out.
Other near-misses to watch for: an outline with a gap (one edge missing), the right shape at the wrong size, or the right shape turned or mirrored.
Run a three-point check on any candidate: (1) every edge is there, (2) same size and same way up as the reference, (3) a clean inside.
Only one shape in each drawing passes all three. If two seem to pass, look again for the line through the middle.
teach.formula: complete edges + same size and way up + clean inside = the hidden figure

worked.stem: In a drawing you find a complete square and a complete triangle, both the right size and the right way up. A line runs straight across the middle of the square; the triangle's inside is empty. Which is the hidden figure?
steps: Both pass check 1 (every edge there) and check 2 (size and orientation).
Check 3, the clean inside: the square has a line through it, so it is a decoy.
The triangle passes all three checks.
worked.answer: The triangle

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Imagine checking a window for cracks.
A good window has all four sides of the frame, and clear glass in the middle.
A decoy window looks fine from far away, but a crack runs right across the glass.
In the drawing, the 'crack' is a line running through the shape's inside.
So for each shape you spot: are all the sides there, and is the inside clear? Only one passes.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's use a three-item checklist, like a pre-flight check.
steps: Check 1: is every edge there? An outline with a gap fails.
Check 2: is it the same size and the same way up as the reference? A turned, mirrored or resized copy fails.
Check 3: is the inside clean? A line running through the middle fails.
Decoys usually pass checks 1 and 2 and fail check 3. That's what makes them tempting.
Only one shape in the drawing passes all three. That's your answer.

example.stem: A diamond outline is complete, the right size, and a line runs across its middle. Pass or fail?
steps: Check 1: every edge is there. Pass.
Check 2: right size and way up. Pass.
Check 3: a line crosses the inside. Fail.

reteach.hook: All edges, right size and way up, clean inside. All three, or it's out.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One small check at a time.
steps: Some shapes in the drawing are tricks.
A trick shape looks right, but it has a line going through its middle.
The real hidden shape has nothing inside it. Its middle is empty.
So when you spot a shape, look at its middle.
Line through the middle? It's a trick. Move on.
Empty middle, all sides there, right size and way up? That's the one.

example.stem: You see two squares. One has a line through its middle. One has an empty middle. Which is the hidden shape?
steps: The square with the line through it is a trick.
The square with the empty middle is the real one.
example.answer: The square with the empty middle

reteach.hook: Empty middle = real. Line through the middle = trick.

army-aviation-information.title: Army Aviation Information
army-aviation-information.blurb: How helicopters fly — controls, rotor aerodynamics, torque, components and autorotation. The one SIFT subtest you can study for directly.

units.title: The flight controls
units.objective: Know exactly what the collective, cyclic, pedals and throttle each do — and how one input leads to another.

steps: A helicopter has four main controls: the collective (a lever by the pilot's left hand), the cyclic (a stick in front, right hand), the anti-torque pedals (feet) and the throttle (a twist grip on the collective).
Collective = up and down. It changes the pitch of ALL the main-rotor blades by the same amount at the same time, so total lift rises or falls together.
Cyclic = direction. It tilts the rotor disc (the tip-path plane), and the helicopter moves the way the disc tilts: forward, back or sideways. In forward flight it is the main airspeed control.
Pedals = heading (yaw). They change the pitch of the tail-rotor blades, which changes tail-rotor thrust and swings the nose left or right.

Throttle = rotor RPM. More blade pitch means more drag, so more power is needed to hold RPM — usually added automatically by a governor or correlator. More power also means more torque, so the pedals must be adjusted too.

Both main-rotor inputs reach the blades through the swashplate. The collective slides it up or down; the cyclic tilts it. Its non-rotating half takes the pilot's input, and its rotating half passes it to the blades through pitch links.
teach.formula: Collective = climb/descend · Cyclic = direction & airspeed · Pedals = heading · Throttle = rotor RPM

worked.stem: A pilot in a steady hover raises the collective to climb. Which other control must the pilot move to keep the nose pointing the same way?
steps: Raising the collective adds blade pitch, so the engine has to deliver more power to hold rotor RPM.
More power into the main rotor means more torque trying to turn the fuselage the opposite way.
The tail rotor has to push harder to cancel it — that is the job of the anti-torque pedals.
With a counterclockwise main rotor (US designs) the nose would swing right, so the pilot adds left pedal.
worked.answer: The anti-torque pedals — left pedal on a US-design helicopter

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Imagine sitting in the pilot's seat. Your left hand, your right hand and your feet each get one job.
LEFT HAND — the collective. It's a lever beside your seat. Pull it up and the helicopter goes up. Push it down and it comes down.
RIGHT HAND — the cyclic. It's a stick in front of you. Push it the way you want to go: forward, back, left or right.
FEET — the pedals. Push the left pedal and the nose turns left. Push the right pedal and the nose turns right.
The throttle is a twist grip on the end of the collective. Its job is to keep the rotor spinning at the right speed.
Memory hook: Collective = Climb. Cyclic = Course. Pedals = Point the nose.
Raise the collective
More blade pitch and lift
More power, more torque
Nose tries to yaw right
Add left pedal

visual.caption: One input leads to another (main rotor turning counterclockwise)

practice.stem: Which control does a helicopter pilot use to move the aircraft forward, backward or sideways?
practice.explain: The cyclic tilts the rotor disc, and the helicopter moves the way the disc tilts. The collective changes total lift; the pedals change heading.

practice.stem: Pressing the anti-torque pedals changes the —
options: pitch of all the main-rotor blades together
speed of the engine and rotor
practice.explain: The pedals vary tail-rotor blade pitch, which changes tail-rotor thrust and yaws the nose. Main-rotor pitch is the collective; disc tilt is the cyclic.

practice.stem: Which helicopter control does the same job as the rudder on an airplane?
practice.explain: Both the rudder and the pedals control yaw — the nose moving left or right about the vertical axis. The cyclic is closer to an airplane's ailerons and elevator.

practice.stem: A pilot raises the collective but no extra power is added. What happens to rotor RPM?
options: It rises, because the blades make more lift
It stays the same, because pitch and RPM are not linked
It falls, because the blades now make more drag
It rises, because the tail rotor takes less power
practice.explain: More pitch means a higher angle of attack, which brings more drag as well as more lift. Without more power the rotor slows — which is why the throttle or governor adds power as the collective goes up.

practice.stem: In straight-and-level forward flight, a pilot wants to fly faster at the same altitude. Which combination of inputs is correct?
options: Raise the collective only, holding the cyclic still
Forward cyclic, lowering the collective to stop a climb
Forward cyclic, raising the collective to hold altitude
Left pedal with more throttle, holding the cyclic still
practice.explain: The cyclic is the main airspeed control: tilting the disc forward adds horizontal thrust. That tilt takes away some of the vertical lift, so the collective is raised as needed to hold altitude. Lowering it would make the helicopter descend.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's follow each control to the part of the helicopter it actually moves.
steps: Every control ends at a rotor. Follow the linkage and you know what it does.
Collective → the whole swashplate slides up or down → every main blade changes pitch by the same amount → more or less lift. Result: climb or descend.
Cyclic → the swashplate tilts → each blade's pitch changes as it goes round → the disc tilts. Result: the helicopter moves the way the disc tilts.
Pedals → tail-rotor blade pitch → more or less sideways thrust at the tail. Result: the nose yaws left or right.
Throttle → engine power → rotor RPM held steady when the load changes.
Big trap: the cyclic does NOT change total lift, and the collective does NOT steer.
Collective → climb / descend
Cyclic → direction
Pedals → heading (yaw)
Throttle → rotor RPM

visual.caption: Four controls, four jobs

example.stem: A pilot in a hover moves the cyclic to the left. What happens?
steps: The cyclic tilts the rotor disc.
Moved left, it tilts the disc to the left.
The rotor's thrust now has a leftward part, so the helicopter slides to the left.
example.answer: The helicopter moves sideways to the left

reteach.hook: Collective climbs, cyclic steers, pedals point the nose, throttle keeps the RPM.

check.stem: Which control changes the pitch of every main-rotor blade by the same amount at the same time?
check.explain: That is the meaning of 'collective' — all the blades together. The cyclic changes pitch cyclically, a different amount at each point round the disc.

check.stem: A hovering pilot wants the nose to face a new direction without moving over the ground. Which control?
check.explain: Turning the nose on the spot is yaw, controlled by tail-rotor thrust through the pedals. The cyclic would move the helicopter across the ground.

check.stem: The part that passes the pilot's collective and cyclic inputs from the fixed controls to the spinning blades is the —
check.explain: The swashplate's non-rotating half takes the inputs and its rotating half passes them to the blades through pitch links. The freewheeling unit is part of the drive train.

check.stem: On a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above, the pilot lowers the collective to descend. To hold heading, the pilot will most likely need —
options: no pedal, because torque is unchanged
forward cyclic, because the nose yaws right
check.explain: Less collective means less power and less torque, so the tail rotor now over-corrects and the nose swings left. Right pedal reduces tail-rotor thrust to hold heading.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One control at a time.
steps: The main rotor is the big set of blades on top. It does the lifting.
Each blade is like a small wing. Tilt its front edge up a little more and it pushes more air down — more lift.
The collective tilts EVERY blade a bit more (or less) at the same time. More tilt = more lift = the helicopter goes up.
The cyclic tilts the whole spinning disc of blades. Tilt it forward and the lift pulls the helicopter forward.
The tail rotor is the small rotor at the back. The pedals make it push harder or softer, so the nose turns left or right.
The throttle keeps the engine — and the rotor — spinning at the right speed.
Collective: up / down
Cyclic: which way to move
Pedals: nose left / right
Throttle: keep rotor speed

visual.caption: What each control does

example.stem: You want the helicopter to rise straight up from a hover. Which control?
steps: Going up means more lift from the main rotor.
More lift from all the blades together is the collective's job.
So raise the collective.

reteach.hook: Up or down = collective. Which way = cyclic. Nose = pedals.

check.stem: To make the helicopter go up, the pilot raises the —
check.explain: The collective adds pitch to all the main blades, so they make more lift and the helicopter climbs.

check.stem: The small rotor at the back of a helicopter is controlled with the —
check.explain: The pedals change the tail rotor's push, which turns the nose left or right.

check.stem: To fly forward from a hover, the pilot tilts the rotor disc forward with the —
check.explain: The cyclic tilts the disc, and the helicopter moves the way the disc tilts.

check.stem: The throttle's main job in a helicopter is to keep the —
options: rotor turning at the right speed
main blades all at the same pitch
rotor disc tilted toward the nose
check.explain: The throttle (usually helped by a governor) holds rotor RPM steady. The pedals point the nose; the cyclic tilts the disc.

units.title: Lift: angle of attack, ground effect & ETL
units.objective: Understand how a blade makes lift and the effects the test loves: induced flow, ground effect and effective translational lift.

steps: Each rotor blade is an airfoil. Its chord line is the straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge.

Angle of attack (AOA) is the angle between the chord line and the relative wind — the air actually meeting the blade. More AOA gives more lift, until the critical angle, where the airflow separates and the blade stalls.

Blade pitch (the angle of incidence) is the mechanical angle the pilot sets with the controls. AOA is aerodynamic: the rotor's own downwash (induced flow) tilts the relative wind and lowers the AOA for the same pitch.
Lift depends on air density, blade area, AOA and airspeed — and it grows with the SQUARE of airspeed. Double the airflow speed and lift becomes about four times as much.

Ground effect: within about one rotor diameter of the surface, the ground restricts the downwash, induced flow drops, AOA rises, and hovering takes less power. It is strongest over a firm, flat surface and weakens over tall grass or rough ground.

Effective translational lift (ETL): at about 16–24 knots the rotor outruns its own recirculating downwash and works in clean air. Efficiency jumps, and the pilot feels a brief vibration as it happens.
teach.formula: Lift = CL × ½ × air density × V² × blade area — double V, four times the lift

worked.stem: A helicopter hovering at 3 feet over a smooth concrete ramp drifts over a field of tall grass and begins to settle, though the pilot hasn't touched the collective. Why?
steps: Over the smooth ramp it was in strong ground effect: the surface restricted the downwash, so induced flow was low and AOA was high.
Tall grass breaks up that cushion of air, so ground effect is weaker and induced flow increases.
More induced flow tilts the relative wind and lowers the AOA on every blade.
Less AOA means less lift for the same pitch, so the helicopter settles until the pilot adds collective and power.
worked.answer: Ground effect is reduced over tall grass, so more power is needed to hover

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of holding your hand flat out of a car window. Tilt the front edge up a little and your hand rises. That tilt against the oncoming air is the angle of attack.
A rotor blade is like a long hand being swung round in a circle. Tilt it a bit more and it lifts more.
Tilt it too far and the air can't follow the top surface any more — lift suddenly drops away. That is a stall.
When a helicopter hovers, the rotor blows air downward. That downward air makes the blades 'see' less tilt, so they lift less.
Near the ground, the ground gets in the way of that downward air, and the blades lift better. That is ground effect.
Fly forward at about 16–24 knots and the rotor moves into fresh, undisturbed air — another boost. That is effective translational lift (ETL).

practice.stem: The angle of attack of a rotor blade is the angle between the blade's chord line and the —
practice.explain: AOA is measured from the chord line to the relative wind — the air actually meeting the blade. It is not measured against the horizon or the mast.

practice.stem: Ground effect is most noticeable when the helicopter is —
options: hovering within a rotor diameter of the ground
cruising level at 1,000 feet above the ground
climbing out at full power well above the trees
descending in autorotation from high altitude
practice.explain: Ground effect appears within about one rotor diameter of the surface, where the ground restricts the downwash and less power is needed to hover.

practice.stem: If the speed of the air over an airfoil doubles while angle of attack and air density stay the same, lift becomes about —
practice.explain: Lift varies with the square of airspeed: 2² = 4. 'Twice as great' is the trap — that would only be true if lift grew in step with speed.

practice.stem: Effective translational lift (ETL) is usually felt as the helicopter accelerates through about —
practice.explain: At about 16–24 knots the rotor flies out of its own recirculating downwash into clean air, and efficiency jumps. A brief vibration is often felt.

practice.stem: With the collective held fixed, which change would REDUCE the main-rotor blades' angle of attack?
options: Accelerating from a hover forward through effective translational lift
Moving from a hover in ground effect to a hover out of ground effect
Descending from an out-of-ground-effect hover into ground effect
Moving from humid air into drier air at the same temperature and height
practice.explain: Out of ground effect the induced flow is stronger, which tilts the relative wind and lowers AOA. ETL and entering ground effect both reduce induced flow and RAISE AOA. Humidity changes air density, not the angle of attack.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's follow the air instead of the blade.
steps: A blade only 'feels' the air that hits it. That air comes from two places: the blade's own spin (straight across the blade) and the rotor's downwash (induced flow, coming down from above).
Put the two together and you get the resultant relative wind. Angle of attack is measured from THAT wind to the chord line.
So anything that adds downwash makes the air meet the blade from slightly above — lower AOA, less lift for the same pitch.
Anything that REDUCES downwash raises AOA and gives 'free' lift: the ground restricting it (ground effect) or flying forward into clean air (ETL).
Ground effect: within about one rotor diameter, strongest close to a firm, flat surface, weaker over tall grass or rough ground.
ETL: about 16–24 knots, felt as a brief vibration and a jump in performance.
More downwash (induced flow)
Air meets blade from above
Lower angle of attack
Less lift, more power needed

visual.caption: Downwash steals angle of attack

example.stem: Why does a helicopter need less power to hover at 3 feet than at 300 feet?
steps: At 3 feet the ground restricts the downwash.
Less induced flow means a higher AOA for the same blade pitch.
More lift for the same pitch means less power is needed to hold the hover.
example.answer: Ground effect reduces induced flow, which raises AOA

reteach.hook: Less downwash = more AOA = free lift (ground effect and ETL).

check.stem: Induced flow is —
options: air pushed down through the rotor by the blades
air pushed sideways out of the tail by the tail rotor
the airflow along the fuselage in cruise flight
check.explain: Induced flow is the rotor's own downwash. It tilts the relative wind and lowers each blade's angle of attack.

check.stem: A helicopter hovering in ground effect over a ramp moves over tall grass. The pilot should expect to need —
options: less power, because the grass cushions the downwash
the same power, because the height is unchanged
less power, because the rotor meets cleaner air
more power, because ground effect is reduced
check.explain: Tall grass breaks up the air cushion, so induced flow rises and AOA falls. More collective and power are needed to hold the same hover.

check.stem: Which of these INCREASES the blades' angle of attack without the pilot moving the collective?
check.explain: Through ETL the rotor leaves its own downwash, so induced flow drops and AOA rises. The other three add downward airflow and lower AOA.

check.stem: During a takeoff from a hover, a pilot feels a brief vibration and a noticeable gain in rotor efficiency at about 20 knots. This is —
options: the onset of retreating blade stall
check.explain: At about 16–24 knots the rotor flies into undisturbed air — ETL. Retreating blade stall happens at high speed; vortex ring state in a slow, steep descent.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from scratch.
steps: A rotor blade is shaped like a wing. Air flowing over it makes lift.
The front edge is the leading edge. The back edge is the trailing edge. A straight line joining them is the chord line.
The air meeting the blade is called the relative wind.
The angle between the chord line and the relative wind is the angle of attack.
A bit more angle = more lift. Too much angle = a stall, and the lift suddenly drops away.
Hovering close to the ground, the ground gets in the way of the air the rotor pushes down, which helps the blades lift. That is ground effect, and it works up to about one rotor diameter high.
Leading edge (front)
Chord line (front to back)
Relative wind meets it
Angle between = AOA

visual.caption: Building the angle of attack

example.stem: A blade's chord line is tilted 6° up from the relative wind. What is its angle of attack?
steps: Angle of attack is the angle between the chord line and the relative wind.
Here that angle is 6°.

reteach.hook: Chord line against relative wind = angle of attack.

check.stem: The straight line from a blade's leading edge to its trailing edge is the —
check.explain: The chord line runs straight from the front edge to the back edge. Span is the blade's length; camber is its curve.

check.stem: If a blade's angle of attack goes past the critical angle, the blade —
check.explain: Past the critical angle the airflow separates from the top surface and lift drops sharply — a stall.

check.stem: Ground effect helps a helicopter most when it hovers —
options: close to a flat, firm surface
well above the tops of the trees
over a field of tall grass
check.explain: The ground restricts the downwash best when it is close, flat and firm. Tall grass breaks the effect up.

check.stem: The air meeting a rotor blade is called the —
check.explain: Relative wind is the airflow meeting the blade. The chord line is a line on the blade itself.

units.title: Forward flight: dissymmetry of lift & blade stall
units.objective: Explain why the advancing and retreating blades differ, how flapping fixes it, and why retreating blade stall limits top speed.

steps: In a hover every blade meets the same airflow all the way round. In forward flight, the blade moving toward the nose (the advancing blade) moves INTO the oncoming air, and the blade moving toward the tail (the retreating blade) moves AWAY from it.

Advancing blade airspeed = rotational speed + forward speed. Retreating blade airspeed = rotational speed − forward speed. Unequal airflow would give unequal lift on the two sides of the disc: dissymmetry of lift.
The fix is blade flapping. The advancing blade flaps UP, which lowers its AOA; the retreating blade flaps DOWN, which raises its AOA. Lift evens out across the disc. (Cyclic feathering helps too.)

Rotor heads allow this in different ways. Fully articulated: separate flapping, lead-lag (drag) and feathering hinges, usually three or more blades. Semirigid: two blades that teeter like a seesaw. Rigid: the blades bend instead of hinging.

The faster you fly, the higher the retreating blade's AOA has to go. Eventually it passes the critical angle and stalls — retreating blade stall. It is a major factor limiting a helicopter's top speed.

Gyroscopic precession: a force applied to a spinning rotor takes effect about 90° later in the direction of rotation. Designers rig the controls to allow for it, so the pilot simply moves the cyclic the way they want to go.
teach.formula: Advancing blade: rotor speed + airspeed · Retreating blade: rotor speed − airspeed

worked.stem: A helicopter's blade tips move at 400 knots and it flies forward at 100 knots. What airspeed do the advancing and retreating blade tips meet?
steps: Advancing tip: 400 + 100 = 500 knots.
Retreating tip: 400 − 100 = 300 knots.
At the same AOA the advancing side would make far more lift — that is dissymmetry of lift.
Flapping (up on the advancing side, down on the retreating side) changes each blade's AOA and evens it out.
worked.answer: Advancing tip 500 knots, retreating tip 300 knots

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Imagine standing in a strong wind, swinging a toy on a string in a circle beside you.
For half of each circle the toy swings INTO the wind, and the air hits it hard. For the other half it swings WITH the wind, and the air hardly touches it.
A helicopter flying forward is the same: flying forward makes its own 'wind' coming from the front.
The blade swinging into that wind is the advancing blade — fast air, lots of lift. The blade swinging away is the retreating blade — slow air, less lift.
To even things up, the advancing blade rises a little (flaps up) and the retreating blade dips a little (flaps down).
Fly too fast and the retreating blade has to tilt so much to keep up that it stalls. That is one big reason helicopters have a top speed.

practice.stem: In forward flight, which main-rotor blade meets the faster relative wind?
options: Both blades meet the same airflow
Whichever blade is over the tail boom
practice.explain: The advancing blade's rotational speed adds to the helicopter's forward speed, so it meets faster air. The retreating blade's speeds subtract.

practice.stem: Dissymmetry of lift is the difference in lift between —
options: the main rotor and the anti-torque tail rotor
the root and the tip of a single rotor blade
a hover in ground effect and one out of it
practice.explain: In forward flight the advancing side meets faster air than the retreating side, so without correction it would make more lift.

practice.stem: How does blade flapping correct dissymmetry of lift?
options: The advancing blade flaps down, raising its angle of attack
The retreating blade flaps up, lowering its angle of attack
Both blades flap up together, raising the whole disc
The advancing blade flaps up, lowering its angle of attack
practice.explain: The advancing blade rises and its AOA falls; the retreating blade drops and its AOA rises. That trims lift on the fast side and boosts it on the slow side.

practice.stem: A two-bladed rotor head that rocks like a seesaw on top of the mast is called a —
practice.explain: A semirigid rotor has two blades fixed to a hub that teeters as a unit. Fully articulated heads have separate hinges for each blade; rigid heads let the blades bend instead.

practice.stem: A helicopter is flying near VNE at high gross weight in turbulent air when the pilot feels an abnormal vibration and the nose starts to pitch up. What is the first corrective action?
options: Apply forward cyclic to hold the nose down and keep airspeed
Reduce collective to lower the blades' angle of attack
Increase collective to restore lift on the retreating blade
Add pedal to stop the roll toward the advancing side
practice.explain: These are warnings of retreating blade stall. Lowering the collective reduces AOA on the retreating blade. Forward cyclic is the trap — it adds airspeed and makes the stall worse. Raising the collective adds AOA, and the roll goes toward the retreating (stalled) side, not the advancing side.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's use numbers to see the problem, then the fix.
steps: Say the blade tips spin at 400 knots and the helicopter flies forward at 100 knots.
The advancing tip meets 400 + 100 = 500 knots of air. The retreating tip meets 400 − 100 = 300 knots.
Lift grows with the square of airspeed, so left alone the advancing side would lift far more and roll the aircraft.
Flapping evens it out: the advancing blade rises (flaps up) and its AOA drops; the retreating blade sinks (flaps down) and its AOA grows.
Fly faster and the retreating blade needs even more AOA. Past the critical angle it stalls: abnormal vibration, the nose pitches up, and the helicopter rolls toward the retreating side.
It is more likely with high weight, low rotor RPM, high density altitude, turbulence and steep or abrupt turns. First fix: lower the collective.
Forward airspeed rises
Retreating blade airflow drops
Its AOA must rise to keep lift
Past critical AOA: stall

visual.caption: Why speed leads to retreating blade stall

example.stem: The blade tips spin at 350 knots and the helicopter flies at 120 knots. What airspeed does the retreating tip meet?
steps: Retreating = rotor speed − forward speed.

reteach.hook: Advancing adds, retreating subtracts. Advancing flaps up, retreating flaps down.

check.stem: The blade tips spin at 400 knots and the helicopter flies at 80 knots. The advancing tip meets —
check.explain: Advancing = rotor speed + forward speed = 400 + 80 = 480 knots. 320 knots is the retreating tip.

check.stem: To balance lift in forward flight, the retreating blade —
options: flaps up, reducing its angle of attack
flaps down, increasing its angle of attack
leads ahead of its normal lead-lag position
check.explain: The slow retreating blade flaps down, which raises its AOA and gives back the lift it lost. Flapping up is what the advancing blade does.

check.stem: Which condition makes retreating blade stall MORE likely?
check.explain: Thin air means the blades need more AOA for the same lift, bringing the retreating blade closer to its critical angle. Low weight, high RPM and smooth air all make it less likely.

check.stem: Because of gyroscopic precession, a force applied to the spinning rotor disc takes effect —
options: about 90° later in the direction of rotation
at the exact point where it is applied
180° away, on the opposite side of the disc
check.explain: A spinning rotor behaves like a gyroscope: the reaction shows up about 90° further round in the direction of rotation. The controls are rigged to allow for it.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One idea per step.
steps: When a helicopter hovers, every blade meets the same air all the way round.
When it flies forward, the helicopter pushes into the air ahead of it.
So the blade swinging toward the front is moving INTO that air. It is called the advancing blade.
The blade swinging toward the back is moving AWAY from that air. It is called the retreating blade.
Faster air = more lift. So the advancing blade would lift more than the retreating one. That is dissymmetry of lift.
The blades fix it by moving up and down — 'flapping'. The advancing blade rises, the retreating blade dips, and the lift evens out.
Helicopter flies forward
Advancing blade: faster air
Retreating blade: slower air
Flapping evens the lift

visual.caption: Dissymmetry of lift, step by step

example.stem: In forward flight, which blade meets more air: the one swinging toward the nose, or the one swinging toward the tail?
steps: The blade swinging toward the nose is moving into the oncoming air.
Its own speed adds to the helicopter's forward speed.
That is the advancing blade, and it meets more air.
example.answer: The advancing blade (swinging toward the nose)

reteach.hook: Advancing = into the wind = more air.

check.stem: The blade swinging toward the front of a helicopter in forward flight is the —
check.explain: It is advancing into the oncoming air, so it is the advancing blade.

check.stem: Different lift on the two sides of the rotor disc in forward flight is called —
check.explain: Dissymmetry means 'not the same on both sides' — the advancing side would lift more than the retreating side.

check.stem: Rotor blades even out their lift in forward flight by —
check.explain: The advancing blade flaps up and the retreating blade flaps down, which balances the lift.

check.stem: If a helicopter flies too fast, which blade is in danger of stalling?
check.explain: The retreating blade meets the slowest air, so it needs the highest angle of attack — and stalls first.

units.title: Torque, the tail rotor & the drive train
units.objective: Explain torque and how it is countered, translating tendency, and how power gets from the engine to both rotors.

steps: Newton's third law: when the engine turns the main rotor one way, the fuselage tries to turn the opposite way. That reaction is torque, and more power means more torque.

The tail rotor makes sideways thrust at the end of the tail boom to cancel torque. The pedals change its blade pitch to hold or change heading. In forward flight a vertical fin also helps carry the load.

Translating tendency: the tail rotor's thrust pushes the whole helicopter sideways in a hover, in the direction of tail-rotor thrust. With a counterclockwise main rotor that drift is to the right; slight left cyclic, often built into the rigging or mast tilt, cancels it.

Other ways to beat torque: two main rotors turning in opposite directions, as on the Army's tandem-rotor CH-47 Chinook (no tail rotor at all), or a NOTAR system that uses fan air blown out of the tail boom. The UH-60 Black Hawk and AH-64 Apache use tail rotors.

The drive train: engine → freewheeling unit → main transmission → main rotor. The transmission reduces high engine RPM to much lower rotor RPM, and it also drives the tail rotor through a drive shaft and gearboxes.

The freewheeling unit lets the rotor turn faster than the engine. If the engine slows or stops, it disconnects automatically, so the main rotor — and the tail rotor, still geared to it — keep turning. That is what makes autorotation possible.
teach.formula: More power → more torque → more tail-rotor thrust (pedal) needed

worked.stem: The engine of a single-rotor helicopter fails in cruise. Why can the pilot still control yaw with the pedals?
steps: The freewheeling unit disconnects the failed engine from the main transmission.
Air flowing up through the descending rotor keeps the main rotor turning (autorotation).
The tail rotor is driven from the main transmission, not directly by the engine.
So as long as the main rotor turns, the tail rotor turns, and the pedals still work.
worked.answer: The tail rotor is driven by the main-rotor transmission, which keeps turning in autorotation

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Sit on a spinning office chair, hold a heavy book out at arm's length and swing it round one way. The chair turns the other way. That push-back is torque.
A helicopter's engine spins the big rotor one way, so the body of the helicopter wants to spin the other way.
The little rotor on the tail pushes sideways to stop that spin — like putting a foot down to stop the chair turning.
Ask for more power (raise the collective) and the body wants to spin harder, so the tail rotor must push harder too. That is what the pedals are for.
The tail rotor's sideways push also nudges the whole helicopter sideways a little in a hover. That is called translating tendency.
Big helicopters like the CH-47 Chinook use two rotors spinning opposite ways, so their twists cancel and no tail rotor is needed.

Freewheeling unit
Main transmission
Main rotor + tail-rotor drive

practice.stem: Torque in a single-rotor helicopter makes the fuselage try to turn —
options: in the same direction as the main rotor
in the opposite direction to the main rotor
toward the side with the advancing rotor blade
practice.explain: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction: the rotor is driven one way, so the fuselage tries to turn the other way.

practice.stem: Why does the CH-47 Chinook not need a tail rotor?
options: Its fixed stub wings produce enough counter-torque
Its two rotors turn opposite ways, so their torques cancel
Its swashplate is rigged to tilt against the main-rotor torque
It uses a NOTAR fan that blows air out of the tail boom
practice.explain: The Chinook's tandem rotors turn in opposite directions, so their torque reactions cancel out. NOTAR is a different single-rotor system.

practice.stem: The main purpose of the freewheeling unit is to —
options: let the rotor keep turning if the engine stops
cut high engine RPM down to rotor RPM
send power from the transmission to the tail rotor
absorb vibration at the blade lead-lag hinges
practice.explain: The freewheeling unit disengages the engine whenever engine RPM drops below rotor RPM, so the rotor can autorotate. Reducing RPM is the transmission's job.

practice.stem: Translating tendency causes a hovering single-rotor helicopter to —
options: yaw toward the side of the advancing blade
settle slowly into its own rotor downwash
pitch nose-up as it moves into ground effect
drift in the direction of tail-rotor thrust
practice.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust pushes the whole aircraft, not just the tail. Pilots correct it with slight opposite cyclic, often built into the rigging.

practice.stem: A helicopter's main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above. While hovering, the pilot raises the collective sharply without moving the pedals. What will the nose do?
options: Yaw left, because tail-rotor thrust rises with collective
Stay steady, because the governor cancels the torque
Pitch up, because the rotor disc tilts aft
Yaw right, because the added power increases torque
practice.explain: More collective needs more power, and more power means more torque turning the fuselage clockwise — nose right. The governor holds rotor RPM; it does not cancel torque. Left pedal is needed to hold heading.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's follow the twist from the engine to the tail.
steps: The engine twists the main rotor. Every action has an equal and opposite reaction, so the rotor twists the fuselage back the other way.
Most US-designed helicopters have a main rotor that turns counterclockwise seen from above. Torque then swings the nose to the RIGHT.
The tail rotor pushes the tail sideways to hold the nose straight. Left pedal adds tail-rotor pitch and thrust; right pedal reduces it.
So: more collective → more power → more torque → more LEFT pedal. Less collective → less torque → RIGHT pedal.

Side effect: the tail rotor's push also slides the whole helicopter sideways in a hover — translating tendency, a drift to the right. A little left cyclic, often built into the rigging, holds it in place.
Power path: engine → freewheeling unit → main transmission → main rotor, with the tail-rotor drive shaft taken off the transmission.
More collective
More engine power
More torque: nose swings right
Left pedal: more tail thrust

visual.caption: Counterclockwise main rotor (US designs)

example.stem: A hovering helicopter with a counterclockwise main rotor keeps drifting right, even with the pedals and collective steady. What is this, and what corrects it?
steps: The tail rotor's sideways thrust pushes the whole aircraft, not just the tail.
With a counterclockwise main rotor that thrust points right, so the aircraft drifts right.
This is translating tendency.
Slight left cyclic (often built into the rigging) tilts the disc to cancel it.
example.answer: Translating tendency, corrected with slight left cyclic

reteach.hook: Collective up, left pedal (US designs). The helicopter drifts the way the tail rotor pushes.

check.stem: On a helicopter whose main rotor turns counterclockwise as seen from above, increasing power makes the nose yaw —
check.explain: More power means more torque, turning the fuselage clockwise as seen from above — the nose goes right. Left pedal corrects it.

check.stem: The tail rotor keeps turning in an autorotation because it is driven by —
options: the downwash from the main rotor
a spring in the freewheeling unit
check.explain: The tail-rotor drive shaft comes off the main transmission, on the rotor side of the freewheeling unit, so it turns whenever the main rotor turns.

check.stem: Which Army helicopter counters torque WITHOUT a tail rotor?
check.explain: The CH-47's tandem rotors turn in opposite directions, so their torque cancels. The other three are single-rotor helicopters with tail rotors.

check.stem: In a hover, translating tendency makes a single-rotor helicopter drift —
options: in the direction of the tail-rotor thrust
straight backward, tail first, into the wind
check.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust pushes the whole helicopter that way. Opposite-to-thrust is the common mix-up.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up.
steps: Push something one way and it pushes back the other way. That is Newton's third law.
A helicopter's engine spins the main rotor one way.
So the body of the helicopter wants to spin the OTHER way. That twisting is called torque.
The tail rotor at the back blows sideways to stop the body spinning.
The pilot's feet on the pedals make the tail rotor push harder or softer. That turns the nose left or right.
More engine power means more torque, so the tail rotor has to push harder too.
Engine spins rotor one way
Body tries to spin other way
Tail rotor pushes sideways
Body stays straight

visual.caption: Torque and the tail rotor

example.stem: If a single-rotor helicopter had no tail rotor, what would its body do when the main rotor spun?
steps: The rotor spins one way.
With nothing to stop it, the body would spin the opposite way.
That is why the tail rotor is there.
example.answer: Spin the opposite way to the main rotor

reteach.hook: Rotor turns one way, body tries the other — the tail rotor stops it.

check.stem: The twisting force that tries to spin a helicopter's body opposite to the main rotor is called —
check.explain: Torque is the twisting reaction to driving the main rotor.

check.stem: What is the main job of the tail rotor?
options: To lift the tail in a hover
To stop the body spinning from torque
To push the helicopter forward in flight
check.explain: The tail rotor's sideways thrust cancels torque and controls where the nose points.

check.stem: The pilot controls the tail rotor with the —
check.explain: The pedals change tail-rotor pitch, and so how hard it pushes.

check.stem: When the engine puts out MORE power, torque —
check.explain: More power into the rotor means a bigger twist back on the body, so the tail rotor must push harder.

units.title: Autorotation, instruments & emergencies
units.objective: Know how an autorotation works and is flown, what each flight instrument reads, and the standard emergency responses.

steps: Autorotation: the engine no longer drives the rotor, the freewheeling unit disconnects it, and air flowing UP through the descending rotor keeps the blades turning — like wind turning a windmill.

Engine failure in flight: lower the collective immediately to keep rotor RPM, use pedal to keep the aircraft in trim (right pedal on a US design — the nose yaws left as torque disappears), and use cyclic to hold the glide airspeed.
Near the ground: flare with aft cyclic to cut the rate of descent and the groundspeed, level the aircraft, then raise the collective to cushion the touchdown using the rotor's stored energy.

Instruments. Pitot-static: the airspeed indicator uses pitot AND static pressure; the altimeter and vertical speed indicator use static only. Gyroscopic: attitude indicator, heading indicator, turn coordinator. The dual tachometer shows engine and rotor RPM; in an autorotation the needles split, rotor above engine.

Other hazards: vortex ring state (settling with power) — a slow, steep descent with power applied; recover by gaining forward airspeed and lowering the collective. Dynamic rollover — rolling over a skid or wheel still touching the ground; smoothly lower the collective.
Performance falls at high density altitude — hot, high and humid air. Take off and land into the wind when you can; it reduces the power required.
teach.formula: Engine failure: collective DOWN → pedal to trim → cyclic for airspeed → flare → cushion with collective

worked.stem: In cruise, the engine of a single-rotor helicopter suddenly fails. What is the pilot's most urgent first action, and why?
steps: Without engine power, the blades' drag starts slowing the rotor at once.
If rotor RPM decays too far, the blades can stall and the RPM may be impossible to recover.
Lowering the collective reduces blade pitch and drag, so the upward airflow can keep the rotor turning.
Then trim with pedal, set the glide airspeed with cyclic, and pick a landing area.
worked.answer: Lower the collective immediately to keep rotor RPM

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture a maple seed falling from a tree. It spins all the way down, slowly. Nothing powers it — the air rushing up through it does the work.
A helicopter whose engine stops can do the same thing. That is autorotation.
The pilot must keep the blades spinning fast. So the very first thing they do is lower the collective — flatter blades are easier for the air to spin.
As the helicopter comes down, air flows up through the rotor and keeps it turning, like wind turning a windmill.
Just before the ground, the pilot raises the nose (the flare) to slow down, then lifts the collective to use the spinning rotor's energy for a soft landing.
Throughout, the pilot watches the rotor RPM needle — it has to stay in the normal range.
Collective down: save RPM
Trim with pedal, hold airspeed
Glide, watch rotor RPM
Flare with aft cyclic
Level, then cushion

visual.caption: The autorotation sequence

practice.stem: Which instrument works on static pressure alone and shows the aircraft's height?
practice.explain: The altimeter measures static air pressure, which falls as you climb, and displays it as altitude. The airspeed indicator also needs pitot pressure; the attitude and heading indicators are gyroscopic.

practice.stem: During an autorotation, the main rotor is kept turning by —
options: the engine, running at its flight-idle power
upward airflow through the descending rotor
thrust fed back from the tail rotor
pressure stored in the hydraulic system
practice.explain: With the engine disconnected by the freewheeling unit, air flowing up through the rotor as the helicopter descends keeps the blades turning.

practice.stem: Which instrument uses BOTH pitot and static pressure?
practice.explain: The airspeed indicator compares pitot (ram) pressure with static pressure. The altimeter and VSI use static only; the turn coordinator is gyroscopic.

practice.stem: In a slow, nearly vertical descent with power applied, the helicopter starts sinking faster even as the pilot adds collective. What is the most likely cause and the correct fix?
options: Retreating blade stall — reduce airspeed and collective
Loss of ground effect — raise the collective even further
Vortex ring state — fly forward and lower the collective
Dynamic rollover — apply opposite lateral cyclic
practice.explain: Vortex ring state (settling with power): the rotor is descending into its own downwash. Adding power only feeds the vortex; flying forward into clean air and lowering the collective gets out of it.

practice.stem: In a steady autorotative descent, the rotor disc divides into regions. Which region produces the aerodynamic force that keeps the rotor turning?
options: The stall region, nearest the hub
The driven region, out toward the blade tips
The whole disc, equally from root to tip
The driving region, between the other two
practice.explain: The driving (autorotative) region, roughly 25–70% of the radius, produces the force that accelerates the rotor. The driven region near the tips acts like a propeller and slows it; the stall region near the hub only adds drag.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's walk through an engine failure one step at a time.
steps: The engine quits. The freewheeling unit disconnects it, but the blades' drag starts slowing the rotor right away.
Lower the collective at once. Flatter blades make less drag, and the air flowing up through the descending rotor keeps it turning — that is autorotation.
Torque has gone, so the nose yaws (left on a US design). Use pedal (right) to keep it straight, and cyclic to hold the glide airspeed.
Watch the dual tachometer: the needles split, and the rotor needle must stay in its normal range above the engine needle.
Near the ground: aft cyclic to flare, cutting speed and descent rate. Level the aircraft, then raise the collective to cushion the landing.
Special case — engine failure in a low hover: do NOT lower the collective. Hold heading with right pedal and raise the collective as the aircraft settles to cushion it.
Collective down: save RPM
Trim with pedal, hold airspeed
Glide, watch rotor RPM
Flare with aft cyclic
Level, then cushion

visual.caption: Engine failure in flight

example.stem: The engine fails at 500 feet in cruise. Put the pilot's actions in order.
steps: 1. Lower the collective to keep rotor RPM.
2. Pedal to trim; cyclic to hold the glide airspeed.
3. Choose a landing area and glide to it.
4. Flare near the ground with aft cyclic.
5. Level the aircraft and cushion with the collective.
example.answer: Collective down → trim → glide → flare → cushion

reteach.hook: Down, trim, glide, flare, cushion.

check.stem: During an autorotation, the needles on the dual tachometer —
options: split, with engine RPM above rotor RPM
split, with rotor RPM above engine RPM
check.explain: The freewheeling unit lets the rotor turn faster than the engine, so the needles split with rotor RPM above engine RPM.

check.stem: The engine fails while the helicopter hovers at 3 feet. What should the pilot do with the collective?
options: Lower it fully at once to save rotor RPM
Lower it halfway and push the cyclic forward
Leave it alone and let the governor recover RPM
Hold it, then raise it as the aircraft settles
check.explain: In a low hover there is no height to glide, so the collective is not lowered. Raising it as the aircraft settles uses the rotor's energy to cushion the touchdown.

check.stem: Which instrument uses static pressure only and shows the rate of climb or descent?
check.explain: The VSI measures how fast static pressure is changing. The airspeed indicator also needs pitot pressure; the attitude indicator and turn coordinator are gyroscopic.

check.stem: In an autorotative descent, which region of the rotor disc acts like a propeller and tends to SLOW the rotor?
check.explain: The driven (propeller) region, toward the blade tips, produces a force that slows the rotor. The driving region, further in, is what keeps it turning.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One small step at a time.
steps: Autorotation means the rotor turns by itself — without the engine.
Think of a pinwheel. Blow on it and it spins.
A descending helicopter has air rushing up through its rotor. That air spins the rotor the way your breath spins a pinwheel.
The freewheeling unit unhooks the engine automatically, so the rotor can spin freely.
The pilot lowers the collective so the blades are flatter and spin easily.
Just before landing, the pilot raises the nose to slow down, then lifts the collective for a soft touchdown.
Engine stops
Collective down
Air spins the rotor
Flare near the ground
Soft landing

visual.caption: Autorotation in five steps

example.stem: Why can a helicopter still land safely after its engine stops?
steps: Air flowing up through the rotor keeps it spinning.
A spinning rotor still makes lift.
The pilot uses that lift to glide down and land softly.

reteach.hook: No engine? Collective down, and let the air spin the rotor.

check.stem: Autorotation lets a helicopter land safely when —
options: the tail rotor is switched off
the pilot wants to go faster
check.explain: Autorotation is the way down after an engine failure: the air, not the engine, keeps the rotor turning.

check.stem: In an autorotation, what keeps the main rotor turning?
options: Air flowing up through the rotor
check.explain: As the helicopter descends, air flows up through the rotor and spins it.

check.stem: The first thing a pilot does when the engine fails in cruise is —
check.explain: Lowering the collective flattens the blades so they keep spinning fast. Raising it would slow the rotor down.

check.stem: Which instrument shows how high the aircraft is?
check.explain: The altimeter shows altitude. The tachometer shows engine and rotor RPM.

spatial-apperception.title: Spatial Apperception
spatial-apperception.blurb: Read the aircraft's attitude from the cockpit view (horizon against a fixed orange aircraft symbol), then pick the outside picture of the plane, seen from behind, that matches. Learn pitch, bank and heading one at a time, then put them together.

units.title: Reading pitch: climbing, level or diving
units.objective: Tell climb, level and dive from the cockpit horizon and from the plane itself.

steps: The cockpit picture is the view through the windscreen. The window, the dashboard and the orange aircraft symbol in the middle never move; only the horizon moves behind them.
Nose up (climbing): you see more sky, so the horizon drops BELOW the orange symbol.
Nose down (diving): you see more ground or sea, so the horizon rises ABOVE the orange symbol.
Level flight: the horizon runs through the orange symbol, about half sky and half ground.

The outside pictures show the plane from behind, flying away from you with its tail toward you. Climbing: the nose (with the propeller) sits ABOVE the tail. Diving: the tail sits ABOVE the nose. Level: nose and tail at about the same height.
The horizon in the outside pictures never moves, so don't use it for pitch. Look at the plane.
teach.formula: horizon below the symbol = climbing (nose above tail) · through it = level · above it = diving (tail above nose)

worked.stem: In the cockpit view the horizon sits well above the orange aircraft symbol, and most of the window shows sea. What is the aircraft doing, and what will the right outside picture show?
steps: Horizon above the symbol means you are looking down at the sea: the nose is down.
Nose down is a dive.
In the outside pictures, look for the plane with its tail above its nose.
worked.answer: Diving: the tail sits above the nose

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: The orange symbol in the cockpit picture is your own aircraft. It always stays in the middle.
Look at where the horizon line is compared with that symbol.
Horizon below the symbol: you are pointing up at the sky. Climbing.
Horizon above the symbol: you are pointing down at the ground. Diving.
Now the outside pictures. The plane is flying away from you, tail first. If it climbs, its nose tips up above the tail. If it dives, its nose tips down and the tail rises above it.

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
practice.explain: Cockpit: the horizon sits below the orange aircraft symbol (mostly sky), so the nose is up: climbing; the horizon is level with the orange symbol, so the wings are level; only sea below the horizon: heading out to sea. Only D shows the plane nose up, with the nose above the tail, its wings level, over open sea. A shows the plane flying level; B has the tail above the nose: diving; C is over land only.

practice.stem: In the cockpit view the horizon sits below the orange aircraft symbol, with mostly sky showing. The aircraft is —
practice.explain: Horizon below the symbol, mostly sky: the nose points up, so the aircraft is climbing.

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?

practice.stem: In the outside pictures the plane flies away from you. How is a dive shown?
options: The tail sits above the nose
The nose sits above the tail
The horizon in the picture moves up
The sea is on the left
practice.explain: The horizon in the outside pictures never moves. A diving plane tips its nose down, so its tail sits above its nose.

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
practice.explain: Cockpit: the horizon runs through the orange aircraft symbol, so the nose is level; the horizon tilts higher on the right against the level orange symbol, so the right wing is down: banking right; sea on the left and land on the right: flying along the coast with the sea on your left. Only B shows the plane flying level, its right wing (on your right) down, with the sea on the left. A has the nose above the tail: climbing; C has the left wing down; D has the tail above the nose: diving; E has the sea on the right.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Use the orange symbol as your fixed point in the cockpit, and nose-versus-tail as the clue outside.
steps: In the cockpit picture, find the orange aircraft symbol. It never moves.
Horizon below it, lots of sky: the nose is up. Climbing.
Horizon above it, lots of ground or sea: the nose is down. Diving.
Horizon running through it: level flight.
In the outside pictures, ignore the horizon (it never moves). The plane flies away from you: climbing = nose above the tail, diving = tail above the nose.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One small idea on each screen.
steps: The cockpit picture is what the pilot sees out of the front window.
The orange shape in the middle is the pilot's own plane. It never moves.
The line where the sky meets the ground is the horizon.
If the plane points up, the horizon drops below the orange shape.
If the plane points down, the horizon rises above the orange shape.
In the outside picture the plane flies away from you. Pointing up, its nose is above its tail.
Pointing down, its tail is above its nose.

example.stem: The horizon is above the orange shape. Is the plane pointing up or down?
steps: Horizon above the shape means the pilot sees more ground.
So the plane is pointing down.

reteach.hook: Up = horizon below the symbol = nose above tail. Down = the opposite.

check.stem: Is the horizon above or below the orange shape?
check.explain: The horizon is below the orange shape, so the plane is pointing up: climbing.

check.stem: Horizon above the orange shape means the plane is —
check.explain: Horizon above the shape means more ground showing: the nose points down, so it's diving.

units.title: Reading bank: the horizon tilts the other way
units.objective: Tell which wing is down from the tilt of the horizon and from the plane's low wing.

steps: When the aircraft banks, it rolls. You roll with it, so the orange aircraft symbol stays level in the cockpit picture and the horizon seems to tilt the OPPOSITE way.
Bank left (left wing down): the horizon's left end rises and its right end drops. You see more ground on the left.
Bank right (right wing down): the horizon's right end rises. You see more ground on the right.

In the outside pictures the plane flies away from you, tail toward you, so its left wing is on YOUR left. A left bank shows the wing on your left lower; a right bank shows the wing on your right lower.
Shortcut: the plane's low wing is on the same side as the high end of the cockpit horizon. Horizon higher on the left? Look for the plane with its left wing down.
A horizon level with the orange symbol means the wings are level.
teach.formula: cockpit horizon higher on the left = banking left = outside plane's left wing down
