worked.stem: In the cockpit view the horizon slopes from high on the right down to low on the left, behind the level orange symbol. Which way is the aircraft banking, and which outside plane do you want?
steps: The ground reaches highest on the right, the side of the low wing: the right wing is down, banking right.
In the outside picture the plane flies away from you, so its right wing is on your right.
Look for the plane with the wing on your right hanging lower.
worked.answer: Banking right: the outside plane's right wing is down

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Cockpit first. The orange symbol stays level; look at which end of the horizon is higher.
Horizon higher on the left means the left wing is down: banking left.
Now the outside picture. Imagine following the plane, like walking behind a friend.
Your friend's left hand is on your left. The plane's left wing is on your left too.
So a left bank shows the wing on YOUR LEFT hanging lower.

practice.stem: In the cockpit view the horizon is tilted, higher on the left. The aircraft is banking —
options: not at all: the wings are level
practice.explain: The horizon rises on the side of the low wing. Higher on the left means the left wing is down: banking left.

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
practice.explain: Cockpit: the horizon runs through the orange aircraft symbol, so the nose is level; the horizon tilts higher on the right against the level orange symbol, so the right wing is down: banking right; only sea below the horizon: heading out to sea. Only C shows the plane flying level, its right wing (on your right) down, over open sea. A has the left wing down; B has the wings level; D is over land only.

practice.stem: This plane is flying away from you, and the wing on YOUR LEFT is lower. Which way is it banking?
practice.explain: Seen from behind, the plane's left wing is on your left. That wing is the low one, so the plane is banking left.

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
practice.explain: Cockpit: the horizon sits above the orange aircraft symbol (mostly ground or sea), so the nose is down: diving; the horizon tilts higher on the left against the level orange symbol, so the left wing is down: banking left; land on the left and sea on the right: flying along the coast with the sea on your right. Only E shows the plane nose down, with the tail above the nose, its left wing (on your left) down, with the sea on the right. A has the nose above the tail: climbing; B has the right wing down; C has the wings level; D has the sea on the left.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Here's a rule you can apply without picturing the roll at all.
steps: In the cockpit, find the end of the horizon that is higher. The orange symbol stays level, so compare against it.
The low wing is on that higher side: horizon higher on the left = banking left.
Now look at the outside planes. Each one flies away from you, so its left wing is on your left.
Pick the plane whose low wing is on the same side as the high end of the cockpit horizon.
Horizon higher on the left: left wing down. Higher on the right: right wing down.

example.stem: The cockpit horizon is higher on the right. Which outside plane do you want?
steps: Higher on the right means the right wing is down: banking right.
Seen from behind, its right wing is on your right.
Look for the plane with the wing on your right hanging lower.
example.answer: The one with its right wing down

reteach.hook: Higher side of the horizon = low wing. Its left is your left.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One small step at a time.
steps: Banking means the plane leans to one side to turn.
One wing goes down and the other goes up.
In the cockpit, the horizon looks tilted against the level orange shape.
If the left end of the horizon is higher, the left wing is down.
If the right end is higher, the right wing is down.
In the outside picture the plane flies away from you, so its left wing is on your left.
A plane banking left shows the wing on your left lower.

example.stem: The horizon's left end is higher than its right end. Which wing is down?
steps: The higher end is on the left.
The wing on that side is down: the left wing.

reteach.hook: Higher end, lower wing. Its left is your left.

check.stem: The horizon's right end is higher. Which wing is down?
check.explain: The higher end shows the low wing: the right wing is down.

check.stem: Is this aircraft banking?
check.explain: The horizon is flat and level with the orange shape, so the wings are level.

units.title: Heading: sea, land or the coastline
units.objective: Read where the aircraft is heading from the ground below the horizon.

steps: Below the horizon you see sea (blue), land (sand-colored) or both. That tells you where the aircraft is heading.
All sea ahead: heading out to sea. All land ahead: heading in over land. These look the same in both views.
Half sea and half land: flying along the coast, with the coastline running straight ahead.
Along the coast, note which side the sea is on in the cockpit view.
The outside pictures look from behind the plane, facing the same way as the pilot, so the sea is on the SAME side in both views.
Sea on your left and sea on your right are different answers. Don't flip it.

worked.stem: From the cockpit, the left half below the horizon is sand-colored land and the right half is blue sea. Which outside picture matches?
steps: Half land, half sea: flying along the coast with the sea on your right.
The outside picture looks the same way as the pilot, so the sides don't swap.
Pick the picture with land on the left and sea on the right.
worked.answer: Along the coast, sea on your right

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture driving along a beach road with the ocean out of your right window.
A friend in the car right behind you, facing the same way, also sees the ocean on the right.
The outside pictures are that friend's view: from behind, facing the same way.
So whichever side the sea is on in the cockpit, it is on that side in the right answer.
All sea = heading out to sea. All land = heading inland.

practice.stem: Below the horizon in the cockpit view there is only blue sea. The aircraft is —
practice.explain: Only sea ahead means the aircraft is heading out to sea. (Diving is about where the horizon sits against the orange symbol, not its color.)

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
practice.explain: Cockpit: the horizon runs through the orange aircraft symbol, so the nose is level; the horizon is level with the orange symbol, so the wings are level; only land below the horizon: heading in over land. Only D shows the plane flying level, its wings level, over land. A is over open sea; B has the sea on the right; C has the sea on the left.

practice.stem: In the cockpit view the sea is on the right. In the matching outside picture, the sea is on the —
options: left, because the view is reversed
practice.explain: The outside view looks from behind the plane, facing the same way as the pilot, so nothing is flipped: the sea stays on the right.

practice.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
practice.explain: Cockpit: the horizon sits below the orange aircraft symbol (mostly sky), so the nose is up: climbing; the horizon tilts higher on the right against the level orange symbol, so the right wing is down: banking right; land on the left and sea on the right: flying along the coast with the sea on your right. Only A shows the plane nose up, with the nose above the tail, its right wing (on your right) down, with the sea on the right. B has the sea on the left; C is over open sea; D has the left wing down; E shows the plane flying level.

Blue means sea.
Sand color means land.

Half blue, half sand: the plane is flying along the coast.
The sea stays on the same side in the cockpit picture and the outside picture.

example.stem: Below the horizon it is all sand-colored. Where is the plane heading?
steps: Sand color means land.
All land means the plane is heading in over land.

reteach.hook: Blue = sea. Sand = land. Half and half = coast.

units.title: Putting it all together
units.objective: Read pitch, bank and heading in order and cross out options one axis at a time.

steps: Each wrong option differs from the right answer on just one thing: pitch, bank or heading. So check all three on every option.

Step 1, pitch: is the cockpit horizon below the orange symbol (climbing), through it (level) or above it (diving)? Climbing planes have the nose above the tail; diving planes have the tail above the nose. Cross out the wrong ones.
Step 2, bank: which end of the cockpit horizon is higher? That wing is down. The plane flies away from you, so its left wing is on your left. Cross out planes with the wrong wing low.
Step 3, heading: sea, land or coast, and which side is the sea on? It's the same side in both views. Cross out pictures with the wrong ground.
One option survives all three. If none does, you misread an axis: re-check the one you were least sure of.
Pace: the real SIFT gives 25 items in 10 minutes, about 24 seconds each; the app's drill is 16 items in 10 minutes. There is time to check every axis.
teach.formula: pitch → bank → heading: cross out on each (outside view: nose above tail = climb, its left = your left, sea on the same side)

worked.stem: Cockpit view: the horizon is above the orange symbol and higher on the right, with sea on the left and land on the right. Which outside picture matches?
steps: Pitch: horizon above the symbol → diving, so the plane's tail sits above its nose.
Bank: higher on the right → right wing down → banking right. The plane flies away from you, so that's the wing on your right.
Heading: sea on the left, land on the right → along the coast with the sea on your left, the same side in the outside picture.
Pick the picture with the tail above the nose, the right wing low and the sea on the left.
worked.answer: Diving, banking right, along the coast with the sea on your left

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Don't try to match the whole picture at once. Ask three small questions, one at a time.
Question 1: is the horizon below, through or above the orange symbol? That's climbing (nose above tail), level, or diving (tail above nose).
Question 2: is the horizon higher on one side? That wing is down, and on the outside plane it's on the same side as you see it.
Question 3: what's below the horizon, and which side is the sea on? It stays on that side outside.
After each question, cross out the pictures that get it wrong.
The last one standing is your answer.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's turn it into a three-question checklist and cross options off as you go.
steps: Read the cockpit view first and say the three answers to yourself: pitch, bank, heading.
Go through the options asking only the pitch question: nose above tail (climbing), level, or tail above nose (diving)? Cross out any that fail.
Go through what's left asking only the bank question: is the right wing down? Cross out any that fail.
Then the heading question, including which side the sea is on (the same side as in the cockpit).
One option is left. Every wrong one fails exactly one question, so you'll always find the reason it's wrong.

example.stem: Cockpit: horizon below the orange symbol, tilted higher on the left, all sea below. What should the matching outside picture show?
steps: Horizon below the symbol: climbing, so the nose sits above the tail.
Higher on the left: banking left, so the left wing is down.
All sea: heading out to sea.
example.answer: Nose above tail, left wing down, all sea

reteach.hook: Pitch, bank, heading. Ask one, cross off, repeat.

check.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
check.explain: Cockpit: the horizon runs through the orange aircraft symbol, so the nose is level; the horizon tilts higher on the right against the level orange symbol, so the right wing is down: banking right; only land below the horizon: heading in over land. Only B shows the plane flying level, its right wing (on your right) down, over land. A is over open sea; C has the nose above the tail: climbing; D has the left wing down; E has the wings level.

options: The one with the sea on the left
The one with the sea on the right
check.explain: The outside picture faces the same way as the pilot, so the sea stays on the left.

check.stem: Here is the view from the cockpit. Which outside picture shows the aircraft in the same attitude and heading?
check.explain: Cockpit: the horizon sits above the orange aircraft symbol (mostly ground or sea), so the nose is down: diving; the horizon tilts higher on the left against the level orange symbol, so the left wing is down: banking left; land on the left and sea on the right: flying along the coast with the sea on your right. Only D shows the plane nose down, with the tail above the nose, its left wing (on your left) down, with the sea on the right. A has the sea on the left; B shows the plane flying level; C has the right wing down; E is over land only.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. Three small questions, one at a time.
steps: Question 1: is the horizon below, through or above the orange shape?
Below = climbing (nose above tail). Through = level. Above = diving (tail above nose).
Question 2: is one end of the horizon higher? That side's wing is down.
The outside plane flies away from you, so its left wing is on your left.
Question 3: what's below the horizon? Sea, land, or both?
If both, which side is the sea on? It's the same side outside.
Find the outside picture that gets all three right.

steps: Through the shape: level.
Flat horizon: wings level.
All land: heading in over land.
example.answer: Flying level, wings level, heading in over land

reading-comprehension.title: Reading Comprehension
reading-comprehension.blurb: Dense, factual SIFT passages. Learn to name the main idea, find details fast, infer only what the text supports and decode words in context — and to spot the true-but-unsupported trap.

units.title: Main idea & author's purpose
units.objective: Name the point of the whole passage and why it was written — and reject options that are too narrow, too broad or never said.

steps: The main idea is the claim the WHOLE passage supports. Each sentence is a brick; the main idea is the wall they build.
Check the first and last sentences of each paragraph. Writers usually state the point there, and the ending often restates it.
Wrong answers come in three kinds: too narrow (one detail), too broad (bigger than the passage covers), and off-target (true in real life but never said here).
Author's purpose asks WHY it was written: to explain, to argue, to describe, to compare or to warn. Words like 'should', 'must' and 'yet' signal an argument.
Tone: pick the mildest word the text clearly supports — informative, admiring, critical, cautious or balanced. Strong words like 'furious' or 'dismissive' need strong proof.

worked.passage: For decades, the captain of an airliner was treated as the unquestioned authority in the cockpit. Junior crew members often stayed silent even when they noticed a problem, assuming the captain knew best. Investigators studying a series of accidents in the 1970s found a troubling pattern: in several cases, another crew member had spotted the danger but either hesitated to speak or phrased the warning so politely that it was ignored. In response, airlines began training crews in what became known as crew resource management. The training teaches captains to invite input and teaches first officers to state concerns clearly and directly. Today the approach has spread well beyond aviation, shaping how surgical teams, ship crews and fire departments communicate under pressure.
worked.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
steps: Trace the flow: old habit (captain never questioned) → problem found in accident investigations → training created → spread to other fields.
'Surgical teams now use crew training' is one detail from the last sentence — too narrow.
'Most accidents are caused by poor communication' goes further than the passage — too broad, and never claimed.
The idea every sentence supports: accidents showed that silent crews were dangerous, so aviation trained crews to speak up.
worked.answer: Accidents showed that crew members' silence was dangerous, so aviation trained crews to speak up — an approach now used in other fields too.

steps: Old habit: captain never questioned
Problem: warnings went unspoken
Fix: crew resource management
Result: spread to other fields

visual.caption: Each step is one brick — the main idea joins all four

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Forget the options for a moment. Read the passage once just to follow the story.
Now give each part a two- or three-word label. Here: 'captains never questioned', 'silence caused accidents', 'training fixed it', 'other jobs copied it'.
Look at your labels together. What single sentence would cover ALL of them? That sentence is the main idea.
Here it's something like: 'Aviation learned that crews must speak up, and others copied the idea.'
Now open the options. Cross out any that match only ONE of your labels — that's a detail, not the main idea.
Cross out any that say more than the passage does, even if they sound true. The one left that covers every label is your answer.

practice.passage: Volcanic ash is one of the most serious hazards a jet aircraft can meet. The ash is not soft like soot; it is made of tiny, glassy fragments of rock. When ash is drawn into a jet engine, the intense heat melts these fragments, which then cool and stick to the turbine parts like a glaze, choking the engine's airflow. Ash also scratches windshields until pilots can barely see through them, and it can clog the sensors that measure airspeed. Because ash clouds are hard to spot on weather radar and can drift hundreds of miles from an eruption, a network of advisory centers now tracks eruptions around the world and warns pilots to route around the danger.
practice.stem: The passage is mainly about —
options: the dangers volcanic ash poses to jets
how jet engines are cooled during long flights
where most of the world's volcanoes erupt
why aircraft windshields scratch so easily
practice.explain: Every sentence describes a way ash harms aircraft or how pilots are warned about it. Engine cooling and windshields are only small parts; eruption locations are never discussed.

practice.passage: Volcanic ash is one of the most serious hazards a jet aircraft can meet. The ash is not soft like soot; it is made of tiny, glassy fragments of rock. When ash is drawn into a jet engine, the intense heat melts these fragments, which then cool and stick to the turbine parts like a glaze, choking the engine's airflow. Ash also scratches windshields until pilots can barely see through them, and it can clog the sensors that measure airspeed. Because ash clouds are hard to spot on weather radar and can drift hundreds of miles from an eruption, a network of advisory centers now tracks eruptions around the world and warns pilots to route around the danger.
practice.stem: The author's main purpose is to —
options: persuade airlines to stop flying near volcanoes
explain a hazard and how it is managed
practice.explain: The passage explains what ash does to aircraft and how advisory centers help pilots avoid it. It never argues for a ban, names no single eruption, and mentions soot only in passing.

practice.passage: Many people picture a military parachute as a simple umbrella of fabric. Modern designs are anything but simple. The round canopies used for mass troop drops are built to descend at a steady, predictable rate, which matters when hundreds of soldiers leave an aircraft within seconds of one another. Ram-air canopies, shaped like a rectangular wing, behave very differently: they glide forward and can be steered with precision, allowing specialized teams to land on a small target miles from where they jumped. Each design solves a different problem. A round canopy trades control for reliability and simplicity, while a ram-air canopy trades simplicity for range and accuracy. Choosing between them depends less on which is better than on what the mission requires.
practice.stem: Which title best fits the passage?
options: How to Steer a Ram-Air Canopy
practice.explain: The passage contrasts two designs and ends by saying the choice depends on the mission. It gives no history, never calls round canopies safer, and gives no steering instructions.

practice.passage: Many people picture a military parachute as a simple umbrella of fabric. Modern designs are anything but simple. The round canopies used for mass troop drops are built to descend at a steady, predictable rate, which matters when hundreds of soldiers leave an aircraft within seconds of one another. Ram-air canopies, shaped like a rectangular wing, behave very differently: they glide forward and can be steered with precision, allowing specialized teams to land on a small target miles from where they jumped. Each design solves a different problem. A round canopy trades control for reliability and simplicity, while a ram-air canopy trades simplicity for range and accuracy. Choosing between them depends less on which is better than on what the mission requires.
practice.stem: The author's attitude toward the two canopy designs is best described as —
options: favoring the ram-air design for its range
critical of round canopies as outdated
doubtful that either design is reliable
practice.explain: The author lists what each design trades away and says the choice depends 'less on which is better than on what the mission requires' — a balanced view.

practice.passage: Supporters of fully automated cockpits point out that most modern accidents involve some form of human error, and they conclude that removing the pilot would remove the risk. The argument is appealing but incomplete. Automation does not eliminate human decisions; it moves them from the cockpit to the design office, where engineers must anticipate every situation in advance. When an aircraft meets a situation no one predicted, such as an unusual combination of failures or freak weather, software can only follow its rules, while a trained pilot can improvise. The record of flights that ended safely because a crew solved an unforeseen problem is long, yet such successes rarely make headlines, so they are easy to overlook. Automation has made flying safer, but the case for removing pilots entirely rests on counting only one side of the ledger.
practice.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's main point?
options: Automation has made flying more dangerous than it once was.
Because most accidents involve human error, pilots should be removed.
Engineers are better than pilots at anticipating emergencies.
The case for pilotless cockpits ignores problems that crews solve.
practice.explain: The author calls the argument for removing pilots 'incomplete' because it ignores flights saved by crews solving the unforeseen. Removing pilots because of human error is the very view the author rejects; 'more dangerous' contradicts 'automation has made flying safer'; and the passage never says engineers out-think pilots — it says they must guess every situation in advance.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's sum it up in one line before looking at the options.
steps: Cover the options. After reading, say the point in one short sentence — under 15 words, like a text to a friend.
Use 'what + so what': what is the passage about, and what does it say about that?
Now uncover the options and pick the one closest to your sentence.
Test each leftover option: does EVERY part of the passage support it? If only one sentence does, it's too narrow.
For purpose questions, find the verb: is the writer explaining, arguing, describing, comparing or warning?
Cover the options
Say the point in one line
Match it to an option
Does every part support it?

example.stem: “Sleep loss slows reaction time as badly as alcohol does. Tired pilots make more errors, and they are often the last to notice. That is why duty-time rules limit how long crews may fly.” What is the main idea?
steps: One-line summary: tired pilots are dangerous, so their hours are limited.
'Sleep loss affects reaction time' is only the first sentence — too narrow.
'Pilots drink too much' is off-target; alcohol is only a comparison.
The option that covers all three sentences is the main idea.
example.answer: Fatigue harms pilot performance, which is why flying hours are limited.

reteach.hook: If you can't say it in one line, you haven't found it yet.

check.passage: Fog forms when air near the ground cools until it can no longer hold all of its water as vapor, and tiny droplets condense out. On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat quickly, chilling the air just above it and producing what forecasters call radiation fog. This kind usually burns off within a few hours of sunrise. Advection fog is more stubborn. It forms when warm, moist air drifts over a colder surface, such as a cold ocean current, and it can blanket a coastline for days. For pilots, the difference matters: a short morning delay may be all that radiation fog requires, while advection fog can keep an airport closed until the wind shifts.
check.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Fog is the single most dangerous kind of weather a pilot can meet.
Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights.
Coastal airports are often closed by fog for days.
Two types of fog form differently and affect flying differently.
check.explain: The passage explains how radiation fog and advection fog form and why the difference matters to pilots. 'Radiation fog forms on clear nights' is one detail; 'most dangerous weather' is never claimed; closed coastal airports is too narrow.

check.passage: Fog forms when air near the ground cools until it can no longer hold all of its water as vapor, and tiny droplets condense out. On clear, calm nights the ground loses heat quickly, chilling the air just above it and producing what forecasters call radiation fog. This kind usually burns off within a few hours of sunrise. Advection fog is more stubborn. It forms when warm, moist air drifts over a colder surface, such as a cold ocean current, and it can blanket a coastline for days. For pilots, the difference matters: a short morning delay may be all that radiation fog requires, while advection fog can keep an airport closed until the wind shifts.
check.stem: The author's main purpose is to —
options: explain how two kinds of fog differ
warn pilots never to fly in fog
check.explain: The text explains causes and effects in a neutral way. It never tells pilots what they must do, criticizes forecasts or describes a particular storm.

check.passage: Before satellite navigation, ships and aircraft crossing oceans relied on dead reckoning. A navigator started from a known position, then used the craft's speed, heading and the time elapsed to calculate where it should be. The method was clever but unforgiving. A small error in measured speed or an unnoticed crosswind would grow every hour, so that a position off by a mile at the start could be off by dozens of miles by the end of a long crossing. Navigators therefore checked their estimates whenever they could, using the stars, landmarks or radio beacons to correct the drift. Dead reckoning is still taught today, not as a main method but as a backup for the day electronic systems fail.
check.stem: Which title best fits the passage?
options: Why Satellites Replaced the Stars at Sea
check.explain: The passage explains how dead reckoning worked, why its errors grew, and why it is still taught. The other titles pick up single words or ideas the passage barely touches.

check.passage: Before satellite navigation, ships and aircraft crossing oceans relied on dead reckoning. A navigator started from a known position, then used the craft's speed, heading and the time elapsed to calculate where it should be. The method was clever but unforgiving. A small error in measured speed or an unnoticed crosswind would grow every hour, so that a position off by a mile at the start could be off by dozens of miles by the end of a long crossing. Navigators therefore checked their estimates whenever they could, using the stars, landmarks or radio beacons to correct the drift. Dead reckoning is still taught today, not as a main method but as a backup for the day electronic systems fail.
check.stem: The author's attitude toward dead reckoning is best described as —
options: respectful but aware of its limits
check.explain: The author calls it 'clever but unforgiving' and notes it is still taught as a backup — respect plus clear limits. Nothing says it beats satellites, and 'still taught today' rules out 'useless'.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Every passage is about one topic. Ask: what is this mostly about? Answer in one or two words.
Next ask: what does the writer say about that topic?
Topic + what the writer says about it = the main idea.
Most sentences in the passage help support that one idea.
A detail is one small fact. It is part of the main idea, not the whole thing.
Purpose means WHY the writer wrote it.
To explain means to teach how or why. To persuade means to argue that you should think or do something.
Words like 'should' and 'must' usually mean the writer is persuading.
Topic: what is it about?
What does it say about the topic?
Put them together = main idea

example.stem: “Camels are well suited to the desert. They can go days without water, their wide feet don't sink into sand, and long eyelashes keep out blowing grit.” What is the main idea?
steps: Topic: camels.
What it says about them: they are suited to the desert.
The water, feet and eyelashes are details that prove it.
example.answer: Camels are well suited to desert life.

reteach.hook: Topic + what it says about it = main idea.

check.passage: Honeybees share the location of food through a movement called the waggle dance. A worker that has found a rich patch of flowers returns to the hive and walks in a figure-eight pattern, shaking her body during the straight middle part of the run. The direction of that straight run tells the other bees which way to fly, measured against the position of the sun. The length of the waggle tells them how far away the flowers are: the longer the waggle, the longer the flight. Using this dance, a single scout can send dozens of workers to a food source she found far from the hive.
check.stem: What is the topic of the passage?
options: how bees build and protect their hives
check.explain: Every sentence is about the waggle dance. The sun and flowers are mentioned only as part of how the dance works.

check.passage: Honeybees share the location of food through a movement called the waggle dance. A worker that has found a rich patch of flowers returns to the hive and walks in a figure-eight pattern, shaking her body during the straight middle part of the run. The direction of that straight run tells the other bees which way to fly, measured against the position of the sun. The length of the waggle tells them how far away the flowers are: the longer the waggle, the longer the flight. Using this dance, a single scout can send dozens of workers to a food source she found far from the hive.
check.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Bees can fly a long way.
The sun moves across the sky each day.
Flowers are hard for bees to find without the sun's help.
Bees use a dance to tell other bees where food is.
check.explain: Topic (the waggle dance) + what it says (it shows other bees where food is) = the main idea. The other options are not what the passage is about.

check.passage: Every recruit should learn basic first aid before finishing training. Injuries in the field rarely happen next to a medic, and the first few minutes after an injury often decide whether a soldier survives. A recruit who knows how to stop heavy bleeding or clear an airway can keep a teammate alive until help arrives. The skills take only a few days to teach and cost very little. Units that train everyone in first aid report that soldiers also feel more confident, because they know they will not be helpless if something goes wrong. For such a small investment, the payoff is enormous.
check.stem: The author's main purpose is to —
options: argue that every recruit needs first aid skills
explain step by step how to clear an airway
describe a typical working day for an army medic
check.explain: The first sentence says recruits 'should' learn first aid, and the rest gives reasons. That is persuading. The passage never explains how to clear an airway.

check.stem: Which word from the passage best shows that the author is persuading?
check.explain: 'Should' tells the reader what ought to happen — a sign of persuasion. The other words just name things.

units.title: Finding details fast
units.objective: Locate stated facts quickly in a long passage and match their meaning exactly — no swapped words, borrowed numbers or changed qualifiers.

steps: 'According to the passage…' means the answer is written in the text. Your job is locating it, not remembering it.
Pick a scan word from the question — a name, a number, an unusual term — and hunt for it or a word that means the same.
Read the whole sentence around it, plus the sentences before and after. Qualifiers such as 'only', 'most', 'until' and 'except' often sit there.
Distractors twist the text: they swap cause and effect, change a number or qualifier ('some' → 'all'), or borrow real words from a different sentence.
The right option usually paraphrases. An option that copies words exactly can be a trap lifted from the wrong part of the passage.

worked.passage: An aircraft's altimeter does not measure height directly. It measures air pressure, which drops steadily as an aircraft climbs, and converts that reading into altitude. Because air pressure at the surface changes with the weather, pilots must set the altimeter to the local pressure reported by the nearest station before takeoff and adjust it during flight. If a pilot flies from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure without resetting the instrument, the altimeter will read higher than the aircraft's true altitude. Instructors teach the memory aid “high to low, look out below,” because the aircraft is actually closer to the ground than the pilot believes. Above 18,000 feet in the United States, all pilots instead use a standard setting of 29.92 inches of mercury, so that every aircraft measures altitude the same way.
worked.stem: According to the passage, what happens if a pilot flies from high pressure into low pressure without resetting the altimeter?
steps: Scan words: 'high pressure', 'low pressure', 'resetting'.
They appear in sentence four: '…the altimeter will read higher than the aircraft's true altitude.'
Read the next sentence too: the memory aid confirms the aircraft is closer to the ground than the pilot believes.
Traps would flip this ('reads lower') or borrow the 29.92 figure, which belongs to the sentence about flying above 18,000 feet.
worked.answer: The altimeter reads higher than the true altitude, so the aircraft is lower than the pilot thinks.

steps: Pick a scan word
Find it in the passage
Read the sentence before and after
Match the meaning, not the words

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Detail questions are a treasure hunt, not a memory test. The answer is sitting in the passage — you're allowed to look.
Read the question and pick its most unusual word or phrase. Here: 'high pressure into low pressure'.
Run your eyes over the passage looking ONLY for those words. Ignore everything else for now.
You land on: 'If a pilot flies from an area of high pressure into an area of low pressure without resetting the instrument, the altimeter will read higher than the aircraft's true altitude.'
Read one sentence further, in case it adds something: 'high to low, look out below' — the plane is lower than the pilot thinks.
Now hold each option against those two sentences. Keep the one that means the same thing. Cross out any that change a word like 'higher' to 'lower'.

practice.passage: The Army's Black Hawk helicopter entered service in 1979 as a replacement for the older Huey. It was designed to carry a squad of eleven fully equipped soldiers and to survive damage that would have brought down earlier aircraft. Its two engines mean it can keep flying if one fails, and key parts of the rotor system were built to keep working after being struck by small-arms fire. Over the decades, the basic design has been adapted for medical evacuation, search and rescue, and transporting senior officers, with each version carrying different equipment in the same basic airframe.
practice.stem: According to the passage, how many fully equipped soldiers was the Black Hawk designed to carry?
practice.explain: 'designed to carry a squad of eleven fully equipped soldiers.' Two is the number of engines; 79 comes from the year 1979.

practice.passage: The Army's Black Hawk helicopter entered service in 1979 as a replacement for the older Huey. practice.stem: According to the passage, why can the Black Hawk keep flying if one engine fails?
options: It is lighter than the Huey.
Its pilots train for engine failure.
practice.explain: 'Its two engines mean it can keep flying if one fails.' The rotor sentence is about small-arms fire, not engine failure; the others are never stated.

practice.passage: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all known marine species. The reef itself is built by tiny animals called coral polyps, which take calcium from seawater to form hard skeletons. Living inside the polyps' tissue are algae that use sunlight to make food, sharing much of it with their hosts; the algae also give coral its color. When the water stays too warm for several weeks, the polyps expel the algae. The coral then turns white, a process called bleaching. Bleached coral is not dead, and it can recover if temperatures fall quickly, but without its algae it slowly starves.
practice.stem: According to the passage, what gives coral its color?
options: sunlight reflecting off the shallow reef
algae living in the polyps' tissue
practice.explain: '…the algae also give coral its color.' Calcium builds the skeletons, and sunlight is what the algae use to make food — both borrowed from nearby sentences.

practice.passage: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all known marine species. practice.stem: Which statement about bleached coral is supported by the passage?
options: It can recover if the water cools quickly.
It covers about a quarter of the ocean floor.
practice.explain: 'Bleached coral is not dead, and it can recover if temperatures fall quickly.' 'A quarter' refers to marine species, not ocean floor, and bleached coral has LOST its algae.

practice.passage: The first nonstop flight across the Atlantic was made in June 1919 by two British airmen, John Alcock and Arthur Whitten Brown. Flying a modified bomber, they left Newfoundland and landed nearly sixteen hours later in an Irish bog, which they had mistaken for a smooth field. Charles Lindbergh is often remembered as the first person to fly across the Atlantic, but his famous 1927 flight was in fact the first solo nonstop crossing and the first nonstop flight between New York and Paris. Lindbergh flew alone for more than thirty-three hours. Alcock and Brown, by contrast, could share the work of flying and navigating, though they battled thick fog and ice for much of their journey.
practice.stem: According to the passage, which statement is accurate?
options: Lindbergh's was the first solo nonstop crossing.
Lindbergh made the first nonstop flight across the Atlantic.
Alcock and Brown flew nonstop from New York to Paris.
Alcock and Brown's flight lasted more than thirty-three hours.
practice.explain: The passage says Lindbergh's flight 'was in fact the first solo nonstop crossing.' 'First nonstop flight' is the popular belief the passage corrects; New York to Paris was Lindbergh's route, not Alcock and Brown's; and thirty-three hours was Lindbergh's time — theirs took nearly sixteen.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's treat it like a word search with a spot-the-difference at the end.
steps: Circle the one word in the question least likely to show up by accident: a name, a number or a technical term.
Jump straight to it. Don't reread the whole passage — run your eyes down the text looking only for that word.
Read a 'window': the sentence before, the sentence itself and the sentence after.
Now play spot-the-difference: hold each option against the window. One changed word ('all' for 'some', 'before' for 'after') makes it wrong.
Beware the option that uses exact words from a DIFFERENT sentence. Right words, wrong place.
Circle a rare word
Jump to it
Read a three-sentence window
Spot the difference in each option

example.stem: “The base gym opens at 0500 on weekdays and 0700 on weekends. It closes at 2100 every day except Sunday, when it closes at 1800.” When does the gym close on Sunday?
steps: Rare word: 'Sunday'.
Window: 'closes at 2100 every day except Sunday, when it closes at 1800.'
Trap: 2100 is right there in the sentence, but 'except Sunday' rules it out.

reteach.hook: Find the word, read the window, spot the difference.

check.passage: Night-vision goggles do not let a soldier see in total darkness. They work by collecting the faint light that is almost always present, from the moon, the stars or distant towns, and amplifying it thousands of times. The light strikes a plate that releases electrons, which are multiplied and then thrown against a phosphor screen that glows green. Green is used because the human eye can tell apart more shades of green than of any other color, which helps the wearer pick out detail. On a moonless, overcast night with almost no light at all, standard goggles show little, which is why many units now pair them with thermal sights that detect heat instead of light.
check.stem: According to the passage, why is the image in night-vision goggles green?
options: Green phosphor is the cheapest kind to manufacture.
Green hides the wearer from the enemy.
The eye can tell apart more shades of green.
check.explain: 'Green is used because the human eye can tell apart more shades of green than of any other color.' The other reasons are never given.

check.stem: According to the passage, when do standard night-vision goggles show little?
options: when they are paired with thermal sights
when there is almost no light at all
check.explain: 'On a moonless, overcast night with almost no light at all, standard goggles show little.' Moonlight and distant towns are light SOURCES that make them work.

check.passage: The Chinook is a heavy-lift helicopter recognized by its two large rotors, one at each end of its long body. The rotors spin in opposite directions, which cancels out the twisting force that a single main rotor produces. Because of this, the Chinook needs no tail rotor, and none of its engine power is spent driving one. The aircraft can carry more than thirty troops, or it can sling artillery and vehicles beneath it on cargo hooks. First flown in 1961, it has been updated many times and remains in service with the US Army more than sixty years later.
check.stem: According to the passage, why does the Chinook need no tail rotor?
options: Its two rotors turn in opposite directions.
Its engines are mounted high at the rear of the body.
It carries loads beneath it on hooks.
It flies only at low speeds.
check.explain: The rotors 'spin in opposite directions, which cancels out the twisting force… Because of this, the Chinook needs no tail rotor.'

check.passage: The Chinook is a heavy-lift helicopter recognized by its two large rotors, one at each end of its long body. The rotors spin in opposite directions, which cancels out the twisting force that a single main rotor produces. Because of this, the Chinook needs no tail rotor, and none of its engine power is spent driving one. The aircraft can carry more than thirty troops, or it can sling artillery and vehicles beneath it on cargo hooks. First flown in 1961, it has been updated many times and remains in service with the US Army more than sixty years later.
check.stem: Which statement is supported by the passage?
options: The Chinook first flew more than sixty years ago.
The Chinook carries exactly thirty troops.
The Chinook has one main rotor and a tail rotor.
The Chinook was retired from Army service soon after 1961.
check.explain: It first flew in 1961 and is still in service 'more than sixty years later'. The passage says MORE than thirty troops, not exactly thirty, and it has two main rotors and no tail rotor.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: A detail is one fact in the passage, like a number, a name, a date or a reason.
'According to the passage' means the answer is written in the passage.
Read the question and pick out its key word.
Find that key word in the passage.
Read the whole sentence it is in.
Pick the option that says the same thing as that sentence.
The words may be a little different, but the meaning must match.
If an option changes a number, or a word like 'all' or 'never', it's wrong.
Key word in the question
Same word in the passage
Read that sentence
Match the meaning

example.stem: “Penguins cannot fly, but they are strong swimmers. Some can dive more than 1,500 feet below the surface.” According to the passage, how deep can some penguins dive?
steps: Key word: 'dive'.
Sentence with it: 'Some can dive more than 1,500 feet below the surface.'
The answer says the same thing.

reteach.hook: Key word → find it → read the sentence → match.

check.passage: The Statue of Liberty was a gift to the United States from the people of France. It was designed by the sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, while the iron framework inside that holds it up was designed by Gustave Eiffel, who later built the famous tower in Paris. The statue was shipped across the ocean in 350 pieces packed into 214 crates. It was put back together on an island in New York Harbor and dedicated in 1886. Its copper skin was once a shiny reddish brown, but within a few decades it had turned the pale green we see today.
check.stem: According to the passage, who designed the statue's inner iron framework?
check.explain: '…the iron framework inside that holds it up was designed by Gustave Eiffel.' Bartholdi designed the statue itself.

check.passage: The Statue of Liberty was a gift to the United States from the people of France. check.explain: '…shipped across the ocean in 350 pieces packed into 214 crates.' 350 is the number of pieces, and 564 adds the two numbers.

check.passage: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity. Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice crash into each other as air rises and falls. These collisions build up electric charge, with positive charge collecting near the top of the cloud and negative charge near the bottom. When the charge grows strong enough, a spark jumps between the cloud and the ground or between parts of the cloud. The flash heats the air around it to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is hotter than the surface of the sun. The heated air expands so fast that it makes the boom we hear as thunder.
check.stem: According to the passage, where does negative charge collect?
options: near the top of the cloud
deep in the ground below the cloud
near the bottom of the cloud
check.explain: '…positive charge collecting near the top of the cloud and negative charge near the bottom.' The top is where POSITIVE charge collects.

check.passage: Lightning is a giant spark of electricity. Inside a storm cloud, bits of ice crash into each other as air rises and falls. These collisions build up electric charge, with positive charge collecting near the top of the cloud and negative charge near the bottom. The flash heats the air around it to about 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, which is hotter than the surface of the sun. The heated air expands so fast that it makes the boom we hear as thunder.
check.stem: According to the passage, what causes thunder?
options: bits of ice crashing together inside the cloud
air expanding very fast after being heated
check.explain: 'The heated air expands so fast that it makes the boom we hear as thunder.' Ice crashing builds up charge — it doesn't make the sound.

units.title: Inference: what the passage implies
units.objective: Draw the conclusion the text strongly supports — one small step, no further — and reject options that are true in life but not proven here.

steps: An inference is a conclusion the passage doesn't state but clearly points to. 'Suggests', 'implies', 'most likely' and 'can be inferred' all signal one.
The right inference is SMALL: one short logical step from what the text says. If an option needs a chain of guesses, drop it.
Point to the proof. For each option, find the sentence that makes it true. No sentence, no answer.
Extreme words (always, never, all, only, proves) are hard to support. Moderate words (some, often, may) are safer — but only if the text backs them.
The biggest SIFT trap: an option that is true in the real world but not supported by THIS passage. Outside knowledge doesn't count.

worked.passage: In the early years of transatlantic air travel, airliners crossing the ocean often stopped to refuel in Gander, Newfoundland, or Shannon, Ireland. Both towns built busy terminals and hotels to serve passengers who might spend an hour or a night there. As engines became more fuel-efficient during the 1960s and 1970s, aircraft gained the range to fly directly between major cities on either side of the ocean. Gander's terminal, once one of the busiest in the world, now handles a small fraction of the traffic it once did, although its long runways still make it a useful place for aircraft to land in an emergency.
worked.stem: The passage suggests that Gander's air traffic declined mainly because —
steps: Find the chain the text sets up: engines became more fuel-efficient → aircraft gained range → they could fly directly across the ocean.
The next sentence says Gander now handles a fraction of its old traffic.
One small step joins them: planes no longer needed to stop there to refuel.
Reject 'its runways were too short' — the passage says they are long. Reject 'travelers disliked the town' — nothing points to it.
worked.answer: longer-range aircraft no longer needed to stop there to refuel

steps: More efficient engines
Longer range
Nonstop ocean crossings
Fewer refueling stops at Gander

visual.caption: The text gives the first links — you supply the last one

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: An inference is like being a detective. The passage never says 'Gander lost traffic because…', but it leaves clues.
Clue 1: planes used to stop at Gander to refuel.
Clue 2: engines got more efficient, so planes could fly straight across the ocean.
Clue 3: Gander's terminal is now much quieter.
Put the clues side by side. If planes can fly straight across, they don't need the refueling stop — so fewer of them land at Gander.
Now test each option: can you point to a sentence that backs it up? If you have to say 'well, maybe…' and add your own idea, cross it out.

practice.passage: Sergeant Ortiz checked the forecast twice before the twelve-mile march, then told every soldier in the platoon to pack an extra pair of socks and a waterproof liner for their rucksack. She also moved the start time an hour earlier and asked the medic to bring additional blister kits. When a private asked why all the changes were necessary, she simply pointed toward the low, darkening clouds building in the west and told him he would be glad of the socks by noon. The private, who had grumbled about the early start, quietly went back to repacking his gear.
practice.stem: It can be inferred that Sergeant Ortiz expected —
options: an enemy attack from the west
practice.explain: She checked the forecast, ordered waterproof liners and dry socks, and pointed at darkening clouds. If she expected a cancellation, she wouldn't move the start earlier.

practice.passage: Sergeant Ortiz checked the forecast twice before the twelve-mile march, then told every soldier in the platoon to pack an extra pair of socks and a waterproof liner for their rucksack. She also moved the start time an hour earlier and asked the medic to bring additional blister kits. When a private asked why all the changes were necessary, she simply pointed toward the low, darkening clouds building in the west and told him he would be glad of the socks by noon. The private, who had grumbled about the early start, quietly went back to repacking his gear.
practice.stem: The private's reaction at the end suggests that he —
options: planned to report the sergeant to an officer
wanted to lead the march himself
accepted that her changes made sense
practice.explain: After seeing the clouds, the private who had grumbled 'quietly went back to repacking his gear' — he stopped complaining and followed her plan.

practice.passage: When engineers designed the first jet airliners, they cut openings with sharp, square corners into the pressurized cabin, much as they had in slower propeller aircraft. Within a few years, two of these jets broke apart in flight. Investigators found that cracks had started at the sharp corners of openings in the fuselage and spread across the metal skin. Each time the cabin was pressurized and depressurized, stress gathered at the corners, weakening the metal a little more with every flight. Modern airliners have rounded windows, and every new fuselage design is tested by repeating thousands of pressure cycles on the ground before it ever carries passengers.
practice.stem: The passage suggests that rounded windows are used today because they —
options: are less likely to start cracks
were first used on propeller aircraft
practice.explain: Cracks began at sharp corners where stress gathered; modern airliners have rounded windows. The link is that removing sharp corners reduces cracking. View and cost are never mentioned.

practice.passage: When engineers designed the first jet airliners, they cut openings with sharp, square corners into the pressurized cabin, much as they had in slower propeller aircraft. Within a few years, two of these jets broke apart in flight. Investigators found that cracks had started at the sharp corners of openings in the fuselage and spread across the metal skin. Each time the cabin was pressurized and depressurized, stress gathered at the corners, weakening the metal a little more with every flight. Modern airliners have rounded windows, and every new fuselage design is tested by repeating thousands of pressure cycles on the ground before it ever carries passengers.
practice.stem: It can be inferred that the problem with the early jets was not caught at first because —
options: the damage built up gradually over many flights
propeller aircraft had suffered the very same cracks
practice.explain: The metal weakened 'a little more with every flight', and the breakups came 'within a few years' — slow, hidden damage. Nothing mentions warning lights, and 'never tested' goes far beyond the text.

practice.passage: The town council expected the new bypass to empty Main Street of traffic, and it did. Trucks that once rumbled past the shops now skirt the edge of town, and the noise has fallen sharply. Yet within two years, four of the street's eleven businesses had closed. The bakery owner, who had welcomed the bypass, now says she underestimated how many of her customers were drivers who pulled over on impulse. The hardware store, which draws mostly local customers who plan their trips, reports steady sales. The council is now studying whether signs on the bypass pointing to the town center could bring some of those passing drivers back.
practice.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
options: The bypass harmed every business on Main Street.
The council regrets the bypass and plans to close it.
Most of Main Street's businesses closed within two years.
Shops relying on passing drivers were hit hardest.
practice.explain: The bakery, which depended on drivers stopping on impulse, suffered; the hardware store, with planned local trips, held steady. 'Every business' is contradicted by the hardware store, 4 of 11 is not 'most', and the council is adding signs, not closing the road.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's use one question on every option: must this be true?
steps: Ask of each option: 'If everything in the passage is true, MUST this be true too?'
If the honest answer is 'probably, if…' with an extra assumption, drop it.
Real-world knowledge is banned. Pretend you know nothing except what's on the screen.
Watch the size of the claim: 'some shops closed' doesn't support 'most shops closed' or 'every shop suffered'.
The survivor is usually modest and stays close to the text.
Take one option
Ask: must this be true?
Needs an extra guess? Drop it
Keep the modest survivor

example.stem: “The flight school hired six new instructors this year, yet it still has a waiting list of students.” Which inference must be true?
steps: 'The school is the best in the state' — needs a guess. Drop it.
'Instructors are well paid' — nothing says so. Drop it.
'More students want training than the school can take' — the waiting list proves it, even after hiring. Keep it.
example.answer: More students want training than the school can currently take.

reteach.hook: Must it be true? If it needs an extra guess, it's out.

check.passage: Arctic explorers of the nineteenth century often carried large stores of canned food, believing that sealed tins would keep their crews healthy for years. Some expeditions nonetheless suffered terribly from scurvy, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C. Expeditions that hunted fresh seal and caribou along the way, as Inuit communities had long done, tended to fare far better, even when their supplies of tinned food ran low. Fresh meat, especially organ meat, contains vitamin C, while the long heating used in early canning destroyed much of it.
check.stem: The passage suggests that expeditions relying mainly on canned food suffered from scurvy because —
options: the tins were often contaminated with toxic lead solder
canning destroyed much of the food's vitamin C
the crews refused to eat seal meat
the cold weather caused the disease
check.explain: Scurvy comes from a lack of vitamin C, and early canning 'destroyed much of it'. Lead in tins may be true in history books, but this passage never mentions it — a classic true-but-unsupported trap.

check.passage: Arctic explorers of the nineteenth century often carried large stores of canned food, believing that sealed tins would keep their crews healthy for years. Some expeditions nonetheless suffered terribly from scurvy, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C. Expeditions that hunted fresh seal and caribou along the way, as Inuit communities had long done, tended to fare far better, even when their supplies of tinned food ran low. Fresh meat, especially organ meat, contains vitamin C, while the long heating used in early canning destroyed much of it.
check.stem: Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: Inuit communities never suffered from any kind of disease at all.
Canned food has no nutritional value at all.
Hunting fresh meat helped protect explorers from scurvy.
check.explain: Expeditions that hunted fresh meat 'tended to fare far better', and fresh meat contains vitamin C. The other options use extreme words (never, no, all) the passage doesn't support.

check.passage: When the base introduced a mobile app for booking range time, officials predicted that phone calls to the range office would fall by half. Six months later, calls had dropped by only ten percent. A survey found that most callers were not trying to book a slot at all; they were asking whether a range was open in bad weather, a question the app did not answer. The office has since added a live status board to the app showing which ranges are open, and the number of calls dropped sharply the following month.
check.stem: It can be inferred that calls dropped sharply after the status board was added because —
options: officials stopped answering the office phone during bad weather
callers could now check range status in the app
check.explain: Most callers wanted to know if a range was open — the one thing the app couldn't tell them. Once the status board answered that, they no longer needed to call.

check.passage: When the base introduced a mobile app for booking range time, officials predicted that phone calls to the range office would fall by half. Six months later, calls had dropped by only ten percent. A survey found that most callers were not trying to book a slot at all; they were asking whether a range was open in bad weather, a question the app did not answer. The office has since added a live status board to the app showing which ranges are open, and the number of calls dropped sharply the following month.
check.stem: The officials' original prediction was most likely wrong because they —
options: misjudged why most people were calling
overestimated how many soldiers owned phones
underestimated what the app would cost
check.explain: They assumed calls were about booking, but the survey showed most were about whether ranges were open. Phones and cost are never mentioned.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Sometimes a passage hints at something without saying it straight out.
Working out that hint is called making an inference.
Example: 'Maya grabbed her umbrella and rain boots.' It never says it's raining, but the clues point that way.
An inference must come from clues in the passage.
It must not come only from what you already know about the world.
Ask: which words in the passage point to this answer?
If you can find those words, the answer is probably right.
If you can't find any words that point to it, cross it out.
Clue in the passage
Another clue
Add them up = what the writer hints

example.stem: “Jamal's hands shook as he opened the envelope. He had waited three weeks to hear from the selection board.” How does Jamal most likely feel?
steps: Clue 1: his hands shook.
Clue 2: he had waited three weeks for important news.
Shaking hands + big news = nervous.

reteach.hook: Find the clues, add them up, and stay inside the passage.

check.passage: At the end of the long training exercise, the soldiers trudged back to the barracks. Their boots were caked with mud, and several of them limped. Nobody spoke on the walk back. When they reached the building, most of them dropped onto their bunks without even taking off their gear, and a few were asleep within minutes. The sergeant looked around the room, smiled to himself, and decided that the inspection he had planned for that evening could wait until the morning.
check.stem: How did the soldiers most likely feel?
check.explain: Clues: they trudged, limped, said nothing, collapsed onto their bunks and fell asleep. They were worn out.

check.passage: At the end of the long training exercise, the soldiers trudged back to the barracks. Their boots were caked with mud, and several of them limped. Nobody spoke on the walk back. When they reached the building, most of them dropped onto their bunks without even taking off their gear, and a few were asleep within minutes. The sergeant looked around the room, smiled to himself, and decided that the inspection he had planned for that evening could wait until the morning.
check.stem: Why did the sergeant most likely put off the inspection?
options: He had too much paperwork to finish that evening.
He saw that the soldiers needed rest.
check.explain: He looked at the sleeping, exhausted soldiers and smiled, then delayed the inspection. Nothing says he was busy or that the barracks were clean.

check.passage: Mr. Alvarez has kept bees in his backyard for twenty years. Each spring he checks every hive, and he keeps careful notes on how much honey each one produces. Last year, his neighbors planted rows of flowering fruit trees along the fence between their yards. By the end of the summer, Mr. Alvarez had collected more honey than in any year since he started. He has already ordered two new hives for next spring, and he has offered to share a few jars with the neighbors.
check.stem: Why did Mr. Alvarez most likely collect more honey last year?
options: The neighbors' new fruit trees fed his bees.
He bought two new hives that year for his yard.
He kept better notes than before.
The summer was cooler than usual.
check.explain: The new flowering trees were planted right by his yard, and that same year he got his biggest harvest. The new hives are for NEXT spring.

check.passage: Mr. Alvarez has kept bees in his backyard for twenty years. Each spring he checks every hive, and he keeps careful notes on how much honey each one produces. Last year, his neighbors planted rows of flowering fruit trees along the fence between their yards. By the end of the summer, Mr. Alvarez had collected more honey than in any year since he started. He has already ordered two new hives for next spring, and he has offered to share a few jars with the neighbors.
check.stem: Why is Mr. Alvarez most likely sharing honey with the neighbors?
options: He has no room to store it.
He wants to sell them more honey.
He is thanking them for the trees.
They asked him to pay for the trees.
check.explain: Their trees helped him get a record harvest, so sharing the honey is a likely thank-you. Nothing mentions storage, selling or payment.

units.title: Vocabulary in context & eliminating distractors
units.objective: Work out what a word means in THIS sentence, and use elimination to finish any question with confidence.

steps: 'As used in the passage, X most nearly means…' — the word often has a common meaning that is WRONG here. Never answer from memory alone.
Cover the word, reread the sentence, and say your own replacement word. Then find the option closest to yours.
Plug each option back into the sentence. The right one keeps both the meaning and the tone.
Use context clues: a definition after a comma or colon, a contrast word (but, yet, unlike), or an example (such as).
Elimination works on every question type: cross out options that are off-topic, too extreme, contradicted or true-but-unsaid. Two left? Reread the exact lines.

worked.passage: Early flight simulators were little more than a cockpit mounted on a platform that could tilt in a few directions. Instructors valued them for teaching instrument flying, but pilots found the experience a poor substitute for the real thing. Modern full-flight simulators are far more sophisticated. They reproduce the motion, sounds and views of a specific aircraft so faithfully that airlines can train a pilot on a new type almost entirely on the ground. Even so, regulators still require a period of supervised flying in the real aircraft, a safeguard against the small but real gap between even the best simulation and the sky.
worked.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'faithfully' most nearly means —
steps: Common meaning: loyally, as in a faithful friend. Can a simulator be loyal? Not in this sentence.
Cover it: 'They reproduce the motion, sounds and views of a specific aircraft so ___ that airlines can train a pilot… almost entirely on the ground.'
My own word: accurately. Training on the ground only works if the copy is very close to the real thing.
Plug in 'accurately': '…reproduce the motion, sounds and views so accurately…' ✓. 'Loyally' and 'religiously' sound wrong; 'frequently' changes the meaning.
worked.answer: accurately

steps: Cover the word
Say your own word
Match it to an option
Plug it back in

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Lots of words have more than one meaning. The test loves picking a word whose everyday meaning is NOT the one used in the passage.
So don't jump to the meaning you already know. Go back and find the sentence with the word in it.
Pretend the word is a blank: 'They reproduce the motion, sounds and views so ___ that airlines can train pilots on the ground.'
Ask: what word would make sense in that blank? Something like 'accurately' or 'closely'.
Now look at the options and find the one that means the same as your word.
Last check: put it into the sentence and read it. If it sounds right and the meaning hasn't changed, you've got it.

practice.passage: The engineers' first prototype of the drone was crude: its frame was made from spare aluminum tubing, and its wiring was held together with tape. Still, it flew. Over the next year the team refined the design, replacing the tubing with a lighter carbon frame and adding a camera that could stream video in real time. By the time the drone was ready for field trials, it bore little resemblance to the clumsy machine that had first lifted off the workshop floor.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'crude' most nearly means —
practice.explain: Spare tubing and taped wiring describe something roughly put together. 'Rude' (a crude joke) and 'oily' (crude oil) are other meanings that don't fit here.

practice.passage: The engineers' first prototype of the drone was crude: its frame was made from spare aluminum tubing, and its wiring was held together with tape. Still, it flew. Over the next year the team refined the design, replacing the tubing with a lighter carbon frame and adding a camera that could stream video in real time. By the time the drone was ready for field trials, it bore little resemblance to the clumsy machine that had first lifted off the workshop floor.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'refined' most nearly means —
practice.explain: The team replaced parts with lighter ones and added a camera — they improved the design. 'Purified' (refined sugar) and 'polite' (refined manners) are other meanings.

practice.passage: Unlike the bold claims in the company's advertising, the engineering report on the new engine was measured in tone. It noted that fuel use had fallen in early tests but cautioned that the results came from only three aircraft flying in mild weather. The authors declined to predict how the engine would perform in extreme cold, where, they wrote, “the data are too sparse to support a conclusion.” They recommended a second round of trials before any airline committed to a large order.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'measured' most nearly means —
practice.explain: 'Unlike the bold claims' signals a contrast: the report was cautious, not bold. It 'cautioned' and 'declined to predict'. 'Calculated with instruments' is the everyday meaning, not the one used for tone.

practice.passage: Unlike the bold claims in the company's advertising, the engineering report on the new engine was measured in tone. It noted that fuel use had fallen in early tests but cautioned that the results came from only three aircraft flying in mild weather. The authors declined to predict how the engine would perform in extreme cold, where, they wrote, “the data are too sparse to support a conclusion.” They recommended a second round of trials before any airline committed to a large order.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'sparse' most nearly means —
practice.explain: The tests used only three aircraft in mild weather, so there was little data on extreme cold — too few results to conclude anything. Nothing says the data were wrong, so 'inaccurate' goes beyond the text.

practice.passage: Historians once assumed that the Roman army's success rested chiefly on discipline and superior weapons. More recent scholarship has tempered that view. Excavations of frontier forts have uncovered detailed supply records, including lists of grain deliveries, boot repairs and requests for extra socks, suggesting that logistics mattered at least as much as courage. An army that could feed, clothe and pay its soldiers reliably could stay in the field long after its rivals had been forced to go home. Discipline, in this reading, was not the source of Roman strength so much as a product of an organization that kept its soldiers supplied.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'tempered' most nearly means —
practice.explain: Newer scholarship moderated the old view: logistics mattered 'at least as much' as discipline, so discipline still counts. 'Hardened' is the metalworking sense; 'rejected' is too strong, because the old view is adjusted, not thrown out.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's turn the word into a blank and let the sentence tell us what goes there.
steps: Treat the test word as a blank. The sentence has a job for it — find the job first.
Look left and right for signposts: 'unlike', 'but' or 'yet' mean the word is the OPPOSITE of something nearby; 'and' or a list means it's SIMILAR.
Say a plain word that would do the job, even a clumsy one.
Swap each option into the sentence and read it in your head. Wrong options sound off or change the meaning.
If two seem okay, choose the one that fits the tone. A calm passage rarely uses an extreme word for a mild idea.
Blank out the word
Find the signpost
Say a plain word
Swap each option in

example.stem: “Despite the storm, the pilot remained composed, calmly reading out each checklist item.” What does 'composed' most nearly mean?
steps: Signpost: 'despite the storm' — she stayed the opposite of rattled.
Clue: 'calmly reading out'.
Plain word: calm.
'Written' (as in composing music) sounds wrong when swapped in.

reteach.hook: Blank it, find the signpost, swap it in.

check.passage: The new radar system was supposed to be a modest upgrade, but its effect on air traffic control proved profound. Controllers who had once tracked aircraft as faint blips that faded between sweeps could now see each flight's identity, altitude and speed on a single clear display. Mistakes that had been common under the old system became rare. One veteran controller, who had been skeptical when the equipment arrived, admitted a year later that she could no longer imagine working without it.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'profound' most nearly means —
check.explain: Signpost: 'supposed to be a modest upgrade, but…' — the effect was the opposite of modest, and the rest shows it changed everything. 'Difficult to understand' is another meaning (a profound idea) that doesn't fit.

check.passage: The new radar system was supposed to be a modest upgrade, but its effect on air traffic control proved profound. Controllers who had once tracked aircraft as faint blips that faded between sweeps could now see each flight's identity, altitude and speed on a single clear display. Mistakes that had been common under the old system became rare. One veteran controller, who had been skeptical when the equipment arrived, admitted a year later that she could no longer imagine working without it.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'skeptical' most nearly means —
check.explain: She was skeptical at first but later couldn't imagine working without it — she had doubted it. Nothing suggests anger or confusion.

check.passage: Early in the campaign, the general's supply lines were tenuous: a single muddy road connected his army to the coast, and a few days of rain could cut it entirely. His officers urged him to wait until a second route could be secured. He refused, gambling that a quick advance would end the fighting before the road failed. The gamble nearly cost him his army when an autumn storm washed out the road for a week and his forward units ran short of food and ammunition.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'tenuous' most nearly means —
check.explain: The colon explains it: one muddy road that a few days of rain could cut. That's weak and easily broken — fragile. 'Lengthy' is a guess from 'lines'.

check.passage: Early in the campaign, the general's supply lines were tenuous: a single muddy road connected his army to the coast, and a few days of rain could cut it entirely. His officers urged him to wait until a second route could be secured. He refused, gambling that a quick advance would end the fighting before the road failed. The gamble nearly cost him his army when an autumn storm washed out the road for a week and his forward units ran short of food and ammunition.
check.stem: Which statement is best supported by the passage?
options: The general's quick advance ended the fighting before winter.
His officers wanted him to wait for a second route.
The general had several good roads to the coast.
Rain had no effect on the campaign.
check.explain: 'His officers urged him to wait until a second route could be secured.' The advance did not end the fighting — the gamble nearly cost him his army; there was a single road; and a storm washed it out.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Some words have more than one meaning. 'Bank' can mean the edge of a river or a place that keeps money.
The question asks what the word means in THIS passage.
Find the sentence with the word in it.
Read that sentence and the ones around it.
Think of a simple word that could go in its place.
Look for that meaning among the options.
Put your choice into the sentence. Does it still make sense?
If not, cross it out and try the next one.
Find the sentence
Think of a simple word
Try it in the sentence

example.stem: “The pilot had to bank the plane to the left to steer around the storm.” What does 'bank' mean here?
steps: It isn't money and it isn't a river — the pilot is doing something to the plane.
Simple word: tilt.
Try it: 'The pilot had to tilt the plane to the left to steer around the storm.' ✓

reteach.hook: Try your word in the sentence. If it fits, it's right.

check.passage: The storm left the small airfield in a dismal state. Branches covered the runway, the windsock had been torn away, and water stood in deep pools across the parking area. The ground crew spent the whole morning clearing debris and pumping out the worst of the water. By the afternoon, the runway was clear, and the first aircraft was able to land safely. The crew chief said it was the hardest morning's work he had seen in years, but he was proud of how quickly the team had restored the field.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'dismal' most nearly means —
