check.explain: Branches on the runway, a torn-away windsock and deep pools of water describe a gloomy, miserable state.

check.passage: The storm left the small airfield in a dismal state. Branches covered the runway, the windsock had been torn away, and water stood in deep pools across the parking area. The ground crew spent the whole morning clearing debris and pumping out the worst of the water. By the afternoon, the runway was clear, and the first aircraft was able to land safely. The crew chief said it was the hardest morning's work he had seen in years, but he was proud of how quickly the team had restored the field.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'restored' most nearly means —
check.explain: After the crew cleared the debris, aircraft could land again — they repaired the field. 'Stored away' is a guess from the word 'store' inside it.

check.passage: Ravens are among the most intelligent birds. In experiments, they have solved puzzles that take several steps, such as pulling up a string to reach a stick and then using the stick to reach food. Ravens also seem to plan ahead: in some tests, birds saved a useful tool for later instead of using it right away, and then used it to win a reward hours afterward. Scientists say these abilities are remarkable because planning ahead was once thought to be found only in humans and great apes.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'remarkable' most nearly means —
check.explain: The abilities are remarkable because planning was thought to belong only to humans and great apes — so they're unusual and worth noticing. 'Easy to mark' is a guess from the word's parts.

check.passage: Ravens are among the most intelligent birds. In experiments, they have solved puzzles that take several steps, such as pulling up a string to reach a stick and then using the stick to reach food. Ravens also seem to plan ahead: in some tests, birds saved a useful tool for later instead of using it right away, and then used it to win a reward hours afterward. Scientists say these abilities are remarkable because planning ahead was once thought to be found only in humans and great apes.
check.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'saved' most nearly means —
check.explain: The birds saved a tool 'for later instead of using it right away' — they kept it. 'Rescued' is another meaning of saved that doesn't fit here.

math-skills.title: Math Skills
math-skills.blurb: No-calculator SIFT math — percent change, rates, algebra, exponents, geometry and long word problems. Early accuracy steers the adaptive test, so build the method first.

units.title: Percents & fractions under pressure
units.objective: Handle percent change, reverse percents, back-to-back changes and mixed-number division without a calculator.

steps: Every percent problem is part = percent × whole. Turn the percent into a decimal (35% = 0.35) or a friendly fraction (25% = 1/4, 12.5% = 1/8, 33⅓% = 1/3).
Percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. Always divide by the ORIGINAL amount, never the new one.
Think in multipliers: a 20% rise is × 1.20, a 15% drop is × 0.85. Back-to-back changes multiply — they never simply add or cancel.
Reverse percent: if the price AFTER a 25% rise is $150, then 1.25 × original = 150, so original = 150 ÷ 1.25 = $120. Divide by the multiplier; don't take 25% off the new price.
Mixed numbers: change them to improper fractions before multiplying or dividing. To divide, multiply by the flipped second fraction.
teach.formula: percent change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100

worked.stem: A jacket is marked up 20%, and then the new price is cut by 20%. The final price is $96. What was the original price?
steps: Both together: 1.20 × 0.80 = 0.96. The jacket ends at 96% of its original price — not back where it started.
So 0.96 × original = 96.

visual.caption: part = percent × whole — cover the one you want

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Start with one idea: a percent is just a multiplier. 20% of something is 0.20 × that something.
If a price goes UP 20%, you keep the whole price (100%) and add 20% more. 100% + 20% = 120%, which is × 1.20.
If a price goes DOWN 20%, you keep 100% − 20% = 80% of it. That's × 0.80.
Now try both on $100: up 20% gives $120. Down 20% of $120 is $24 off, which leaves $96. Not $100!
The drop was bigger because 20% of $120 is more than 20% of $100. That's why two equal changes never cancel out.
So 'up 20% then down 20%' always means × 0.96. If the end price is $96, the start price was 96 ÷ 0.96 = $100.
Golden rule for going backwards: DIVIDE by the multiplier. Never subtract the percent from the new number.

practice.stem: What is 15% of 260?
A part's price falls from $80 to $68. What is the percent decrease?
practice.explain: Change = 80 − 68 = 12. Divide by the OLD price: 12 ÷ 80 = 0.15 = 15%. 12 ÷ 68 ≈ 17.6% wrongly divides by the new price; 12% is the dollar drop, not a percent.
2 2/3 = 8/3 and 1 1/9 = 10/9. Flip and multiply: 8/3 × 9/10 = 72/30 = 12/5 = 2 2/5. 2 26/27 multiplies without flipping; 8 divides the wholes and fractions separately (2 ÷ 1 and 2/3 ÷ 1/9 = 6).

practice.stem: After a 25% raise, a technician earns $3,500 a month. What was the monthly pay before the raise?
practice.explain: 1.25 × old = 3,500, so old = 3,500 ÷ 1.25 = 2,800. Taking 25% off $3,500 ($2,625) uses the wrong base — 25% of the NEW pay is bigger than 25% of the old pay.

practice.stem: A unit's budget rose 10% in year one and another 20% in year two, ending at $66,000. What was the budget at the start?
practice.explain: Multipliers multiply: 1.10 × 1.20 = 1.32. Start = 66,000 ÷ 1.32 = 50,000. About $50,770 wrongly adds the changes to 30% (66,000 ÷ 1.30); $47,520 subtracts the percents from the end figure instead of dividing.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's turn every percent into a multiplier and test it on $100.
steps: When no starting number is given, pretend it was $100 — percents are easiest with 100.
Up 20% takes $100 to $120. Down 20% then takes 20% of $120 = $24 off, leaving $96. Equal ups and downs never cancel.
That's why multipliers win: up 20% is × 1.2, down 20% is × 0.8, and 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 — a 4% loss overall.
Going backwards? Undo a multiplier by DIVIDING by it. After a 25% rise you have 1.25 × the original, so divide by 1.25.
Percent change always compares with where you STARTED: change ÷ old.
Fractions follow the same logic: 'of' means ×, and dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip (÷ 2/3 = × 3/2).

visual.caption: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, so 4% is lost overall

example.stem: After a 40% discount, a headset costs $54. What was the original price?
steps: 40% off leaves 60% of the price, so the multiplier is 0.6.
0.6 × original = 54.

reteach.hook: Multipliers multiply. To go back, divide by the multiplier.

check.explain: 7/2 ÷ 7/4 = 7/2 × 4/7 = 28/14 = 2. 6 1/8 multiplies without flipping; 3 2/3 divides the wholes and fractions separately; 1/2 flips the wrong fraction.

check.stem: After a 15% discount, a radio costs $68. What was the original price?
check.explain: 0.85 × original = 68, so original = 68 ÷ 0.85 = 80. $78.20 adds 15% of $68 back on — the wrong base.

check.stem: Enrollment grew from 250 to 320. What was the percent increase?
check.explain: Change = 70. Divide by the OLD number: 70 ÷ 250 = 0.28 = 28%. About 21.9% divides by 320; 128% is the new number as a percent of the old.

check.stem: A value drops 50% and then rises 50%. Compared with the start, it is now —
check.explain: 0.5 × 1.5 = 0.75, so it ends at 75% of the start: 25% lower. On $100: down to $50, then up $25 to $75.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Percent means 'out of 100'. 30% means 30 out of every 100.
To turn a percent into a decimal, move the point two places left: 30% = 0.30.
'Of' means multiply. 30% of 50 = 0.30 × 50 = 15.
A 10% rise means you keep all 100% and add 10%: that's 110%, or × 1.10.
A 10% drop means you keep 90%: that's × 0.90.
For percent change, first find the change: new minus old.
Then divide the change by the OLD number and turn it into a percent.
If you know the amount AFTER a change, divide by the multiplier to get back to the start.

example.stem: A tool kit costs $40, then the price goes up 15%. What is the new price?
steps: 15% as a decimal is 0.15.
New price = 40 + 6 = 46.
Or in one go: 40 × 1.15 = 46.

reteach.hook: Percent → decimal → multiply. For change, divide by the OLD number.

check.stem: What is 0.6% written as a decimal?
check.explain: Move the point two places left: 0.6% → 0.006. 0.06 only moves it one place; 0.0006 moves it three.

check.stem: What is 20% of 45?
A bill rises from $60 to $75. What is the percent increase?
check.explain: Change = 15. 15 ÷ 60 (the OLD amount) = 0.25 = 25%. 20% divides by the new amount, 75.

check.stem: Which multiplier gives a 35% decrease?
check.explain: A 35% drop leaves 100% − 35% = 65%, so × 0.65. × 0.35 would leave only 35% — a 65% drop.

units.title: Ratios, proportions & rates
units.objective: Split totals by ratio, scale with proportions, and solve work-rate and average-speed problems.

steps: A ratio a : b means a + b equal shares. Find ONE share = total ÷ (a + b), then multiply out.
A proportion is two equal fractions. Keep matching units in matching places (cost on top, items underneath on both sides), then cross-multiply.
Direct or inverse? More items cost more (direct). But more workers on a FIXED job finish sooner: workers × days stays constant (inverse).
Work rate: a worker who takes 6 hours does 1/6 of the job each hour. Add the hourly rates to work together: 1/a + 1/b = 1/T.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. It is NOT the average of the two speeds, because you spend longer at the slower speed.
teach.formula: together: 1/T = 1/a + 1/b

worked.stem: One pump fills a fuel tank in 6 hours; a second pump fills it in 3 hours. Working together, how long do they take?
steps: Pump A does 1/6 of the tank per hour. Pump B does 1/3 = 2/6 per hour.
Together: 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 of the tank per hour.
Half a tank each hour → the whole tank takes 2 hours.
Shortcut for two workers: (a × b) ÷ (a + b) = 18 ÷ 9 = 2 ✓.
worked.answer: 2 hours

visual.caption: Each hour: A fills 1 sixth, B fills 2 sixths — together half the tank

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Fractions of a tank feel slippery, so let's give the tank a size. Pick a number both 6 and 3 divide into — 6 works. Say the tank holds 6 units.
Pump A fills 6 units in 6 hours. That's 1 unit every hour.
Pump B fills 6 units in 3 hours. That's 2 units every hour.
Running together, every hour they add 1 + 2 = 3 units.
The tank needs 6 units. 6 ÷ 3 = 2 hours.
Notice the answer is LESS than the faster pump's 3 hours. Two pumps together must beat either one alone — a quick way to spot wrong options.

practice.stem: Fuel and oil are mixed in the ratio 7 : 2. How much oil goes into 36 gallons of the mix?
practice.explain: 7 + 2 = 9 shares. One share = 36 ÷ 9 = 4 gal. Oil = 2 shares = 8 gal. 28 gal is the fuel; about 10.3 treats 2 : 7 as a fraction of the whole (36 × 2/7).

practice.stem: If 5 identical sensors cost $340, how much do 8 cost?
practice.explain: One sensor = 340 ÷ 5 = $68. Eight = 8 × 68 = $544. $212.50 flips the proportion (340 × 5/8).

practice.stem: A map's scale is 1 inch : 12 miles. Two bases are 4 3/4 inches apart on the map. What is the real distance?
practice.explain: 4 3/4 × 12 = 4 × 12 + 3/4 × 12 = 48 + 9 = 57 miles. 48.75 forgets to scale the 3/4; 51 adds 3 instead of 3/4 × 12.

practice.stem: Six mechanics can service a fleet in 10 days. At the same rate, how many days would 4 mechanics take?
practice.explain: The job is fixed: 6 × 10 = 60 mechanic-days. 60 ÷ 4 = 15 days. Fewer workers must take LONGER, so 6.7 (a direct proportion) can't be right.

practice.stem: A helicopter flies 240 miles out at 120 mph and returns the same 240 miles at 80 mph. What is its average speed for the round trip?
practice.explain: Out: 240 ÷ 120 = 2 h. Back: 240 ÷ 80 = 3 h. Total 480 miles ÷ 5 h = 96 mph. 100 averages the speeds; 48 divides only one leg's distance by the total time.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's give every job a size so the fractions turn into whole numbers.
steps: Work problems: invent a job size that every time in the question divides into. A 12-hour crew and a 4-hour team? Call the job 12 units.
Now each worker has a plain speed in units per hour, and speeds working together simply add.
Fixed job, more workers: workers × time never changes. 6 mechanics × 10 days = 60 mechanic-days, however you split it.
Ratios: draw the shares. 7 : 2 is 9 equal blocks, and one block = total ÷ 9.
Average speed: find each leg's time, add the times, then total distance ÷ total time.

visual.caption: Job = 12 units. Together they do 3 an hour, A does 1, so B does 2

example.stem: Crew A can refuel a fleet alone in 12 hours. Crews A and B together take 4 hours. How long would crew B take alone?
steps: Call the job 12 units (12 and 4 both divide into it).
Together: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 units an hour. Crew A alone: 12 ÷ 12 = 1 unit an hour.
So crew B must do 3 − 1 = 2 units an hour.
B alone: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 hours.

reteach.hook: Give the job a size. Then it's just units per hour.

check.stem: Pipe A drains a tank in 4 hours and pipe B drains it in 12 hours. How long do they take together?
check.explain: Call the tank 12 units: A drains 3 an hour, B drains 1, together 4. 12 ÷ 4 = 3 h. 8 averages the times; any answer longer than 4 h is slower than A alone, which is impossible.

check.stem: A runner covers 6 miles at 6 mph, then another 6 miles at 3 mph. What is the average speed for the whole run?
check.explain: Times: 6 ÷ 6 = 1 h and 6 ÷ 3 = 2 h. Total 12 miles ÷ 3 h = 4 mph. 4.5 averages the speeds, ignoring that the slow leg took twice as long.

check.stem: Eight workers build a wall in 9 days. How many days would 12 workers take?
check.explain: Job = 8 × 9 = 72 worker-days. 72 ÷ 12 = 6 days. 13.5 scales the wrong way — more workers must finish sooner.

check.stem: Sand and gravel are mixed 3 : 5 to make 72 tons. How many more tons of gravel than sand are there?
check.explain: 8 shares, so one share = 72 ÷ 8 = 9 tons. Sand = 27, gravel = 45, difference = 18 tons (two shares). 45 is the gravel alone; 9 is a single share.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: A ratio compares two amounts. 3 : 5 means 'for every 3 of the first, there are 5 of the second'.
Add the two numbers to get the number of equal shares: 3 + 5 = 8.
Divide the total by the number of shares to get ONE share.
Multiply one share by each number in the ratio.
A rate is an amount for each one unit of time, like 50 miles per hour.
To find a speed, divide: miles ÷ hours.
To find a time, divide: miles ÷ speed.
For an average speed, add up ALL the miles and ALL the hours, then divide.

visual.caption: 8 blocks share 40 recruits, so each block = 5

example.stem: 40 recruits are split between two platoons in the ratio 3 : 5. How many are in the smaller platoon?
steps: Shares: 3 + 5 = 8.
One share: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 recruits.
Smaller platoon = 3 shares = 3 × 5 = 15.
Check: the other platoon is 5 × 5 = 25, and 15 + 25 = 40 ✓.

reteach.hook: Add the parts, find one share, multiply out.

check.stem: In the ratio 4 : 1, how many equal shares are there in total?
check.explain: Add the parts: 4 + 1 = 5 shares.

check.stem: $90 is split in the ratio 2 : 1. How much is the larger share?
check.explain: 3 shares, so one share = 90 ÷ 3 = $30. The larger part is 2 shares = $60. $30 is only one share.

check.stem: A truck travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. What is its average speed?
check.explain: Speed = miles ÷ hours = 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 mph. 375 multiplies instead of dividing.

check.stem: A cyclist rides 20 miles in 2 hours, then 10 miles in half an hour. What is the average speed for the whole ride?
check.explain: All the miles: 30. All the hours: 2.5. 30 ÷ 2.5 = 12 mph. 15 averages the two speeds (10 and 20), which ignores how long each part took.

units.title: Linear equations & inequalities
units.objective: Solve equations with x on both sides or in fractions, flip inequalities correctly and handle compound inequalities.

steps: Goal: get x alone. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other — the balance stays level.
x on both sides? Subtract the smaller x-term from both sides so x lives on one side, then move the numbers across.
Fractions? Multiply EVERY term on both sides by the common denominator first. The fractions disappear.
Inequalities (<, >, ≤, ≥) solve the same way with one extra rule: multiply or divide by a NEGATIVE and the sign flips.
A compound inequality like −7 ≤ (3 − 2x)/5 < 1 has three parts. Do every step to all three at once.
Check by plugging your answer back in. Ten seconds catches most sign slips.
teach.formula: ÷ or × by a negative → flip the inequality sign

worked.stem: Solve x/3 + 4 = x/2 − 1.
steps: The denominators are 3 and 2, so multiply every term by 6.
Subtract 2x from both sides: 24 = x − 6.
Add 6 to both sides: x = 30.

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture the equation as a balance scale. Both pans weigh the same. Any move you make to one pan, you make to the other.
Fractions are awkward, so first get rid of them. 3 and 2 both go into 6, so multiply EVERYTHING by 6 — every single term, on both sides.
x/3 × 6 = 2x. 4 × 6 = 24. x/2 × 6 = 3x. 1 × 6 = 6. Now it reads 2x + 24 = 3x − 6. No fractions left.
There are x's on both pans. Take 2x off each: the left becomes 24, the right becomes x − 6.
x has 6 taken away from it. Undo that by adding 6 to both sides: 24 + 6 = x, so x = 30.
Inequalities work exactly the same — except if you ever multiply or divide both sides by a negative number, turn the sign around.
Why? 2 < 3 is true, but times −1 gives −2 and −3, and −2 is BIGGER than −3. The order flips, so the sign must flip.

practice.stem: Solve 4x + 9 = 37.
practice.explain: Subtract 9: 4x = 28. Divide by 4: x = 7. 11.5 adds the 9 instead of subtracting it; 28 forgets to divide.

practice.stem: Solve 7x − 5 = 3x + 19.
practice.explain: Subtract 3x: 4x − 5 = 19. Add 5: 4x = 24. Divide: x = 6. 3.5 moves the 5 with the wrong sign; 2.4 adds the x-terms (10x) instead of subtracting.

practice.stem: Solve x/4 + 3 = x/6 + 5.
practice.explain: Multiply every term by 12: 3x + 36 = 2x + 60. Subtract 2x and 36: x = 24. Check: 6 + 3 = 9 and 4 + 5 = 9 ✓. 4.8 comes from adding x/4 and x/6 instead of subtracting.

practice.stem: Solve −3x + 8 > 20.
practice.explain: Subtract 8: −3x > 12. Divide by −3 and FLIP: x < −4. Check x = −5: 15 + 8 = 23 > 20 ✓. x > −4 forgets the flip.

practice.stem: Which values of x satisfy −7 ≤ (3 − 2x)/5 < 1?
practice.explain: × 5: −35 ≤ 3 − 2x < 5. − 3: −38 ≤ −2x < 2. ÷ −2 and flip both signs: 19 ≥ x > −1, i.e. −1 < x ≤ 19. Check x = 19: (3 − 38)/5 = −7 ✓ (included); x = −1 gives exactly 1, which is not < 1, so −1 is excluded. −1 ≤ x < 19 puts the 'or equal to' on the wrong ends.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's treat solving as undoing — and test inequalities with a real number.
steps: An equation is a recipe done to x. Solving means undoing the recipe in reverse order.
Collect first: if x is on both sides, subtract the smaller x-term from both sides so x lives on one side only.
Clear fractions next: multiply EVERY term by the common denominator. x/2 − 3 = x/5 + 3 becomes 5x − 30 = 2x + 30.
Inequalities use the same moves. But dividing by a negative turns the number line around, so the sign flips: 2 < 3, yet −2 > −3.
Not sure about the direction? Pick a number from your answer and plug it into the ORIGINAL inequality. If it fails, flip.

visual.caption: Every value at −3 or to its left works

example.stem: Solve 5 − 2x ≥ 11.
steps: Subtract 5 from both sides: −2x ≥ 6.
Divide both sides by −2. Dividing by a negative flips the sign: x ≤ −3.
Test x = −4 (should work): 5 − 2(−4) = 13, and 13 ≥ 11 ✓.
Test x = 0 (should fail): 5 ≥ 11 is false ✓. The direction is right.

reteach.hook: Divide by a negative? Flip the sign — then test a number.

check.stem: Solve 9 − 4x < 1.
check.explain: Subtract 9: −4x < −8. Divide by −4 and flip: x > 2. Test x = 3: 9 − 12 = −3 < 1 ✓. x < 2 forgets the flip.

check.stem: Solve 3(x − 2) = x + 10.
check.explain: Expand: 3x − 6 = x + 10. Subtract x: 2x − 6 = 10. Add 6: 2x = 16. x = 8. 6 forgets to multiply the 2 by 3; 16 forgets to divide.

check.stem: If f(x) = 3x² − 2x + 5, what is f(−3)?
check.explain: 3(−3)² = 3 × 9 = 27; −2(−3) = +6; then + 5. 27 + 6 + 5 = 38. 26 misses that −2 × −3 is positive; 92 squares 3 × −3 instead of just −3.

check.stem: Solve x/2 − 3 = x/5 + 3.
check.explain: Multiply every term by 10: 5x − 30 = 2x + 30. Subtract 2x and add 30: 3x = 60, so x = 20. Check: 10 − 3 = 7 and 4 + 3 = 7 ✓. 60 forgets to divide by 3.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: An equation says two things are equal, like a balance scale that is level.
Whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other side.
To undo + 7, subtract 7. To undo − 7, add 7.
To undo × 3, divide by 3. To undo ÷ 3, multiply by 3.
Undo the adding and subtracting first, then the multiplying and dividing.
An inequality uses <, >, ≤ or ≥ instead of =.
You solve it just like an equation.
One extra rule: if you multiply or divide by a negative number, flip the sign around.

example.stem: Solve 3x + 7 = 22.
steps: Undo + 7: subtract 7 from both sides → 3x = 15.
Undo × 3: divide both sides by 3 → x = 5.

reteach.hook: Do it to both sides. Divide by a negative? Flip the sign.

check.stem: Solve x − 9 = 14.
check.explain: Undo − 9 by adding 9 to both sides: x = 14 + 9 = 23.

check.stem: Solve 6x = 42.
check.explain: Undo × 6 by dividing both sides by 6: x = 42 ÷ 6 = 7.

check.stem: Solve 2x + 5 = 17.
check.explain: Subtract 5: 2x = 12. Divide by 2: x = 6. 12 forgets to divide; 11 adds the 5 instead of subtracting.

check.stem: Solve −2x > 8.
check.explain: Divide both sides by −2 and flip the sign: x < −4. Test x = −5: −2 × −5 = 10 > 8 ✓.

units.title: Exponents, roots & scientific notation
units.objective: Use the exponent laws, simplify square roots, and calculate in scientific notation by hand.

steps: Same base: multiplying → ADD the powers (x³ · x⁴ = x⁷). Dividing → SUBTRACT (x⁹ ÷ x⁴ = x⁵). Power of a power → MULTIPLY ((x³)² = x⁶).
x⁰ = 1, and a negative power means 'one over': x⁻² = 1/x². A negative exponent never makes the number negative.
Simplify a root by pulling out the biggest perfect square: √72 = √(36 × 2) = 6√2. Only like roots add: 3√2 + 5√2 = 8√2.
Scientific notation = a number from 1 up to (not including) 10, times a power of ten: 45,000 = 4.5 × 10⁴ and 0.0062 = 6.2 × 10⁻³.
To multiply or divide in scientific notation, handle the front numbers and the powers of ten separately, then re-adjust so the front is between 1 and 10.
teach.formula: multiply → add powers · divide → subtract · bracket → multiply

worked.stem: Write (6 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10⁻²) in scientific notation.
steps: Front numbers: 6 × 4 = 24.
Powers of ten: 10⁵ × 10⁻² = 10³ (add the powers: 5 + (−2) = 3).
So far: 24 × 10³ — but 24 is not between 1 and 10.
Multiply the front numbers
Add the powers of ten
Front not 1–9.99? Shift the point
Adjust the power to match

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Scientific notation is just a tidy way to write very big or very small numbers: one short number, times 10 to some power.
10⁵ means 1 followed by five zeros: 100,000. 10⁻² means 'one over 10²', which is 1/100 = 0.01.
To multiply (6 × 10⁵) by (4 × 10⁻²), you can rearrange the multiplication: (6 × 4) × (10⁵ × 10⁻²).
6 × 4 = 24. And 10⁵ × 10⁻² means multiply by 100,000 then by 0.01 — that's the same as 10³. Adding the powers (5 + −2 = 3) gives the same thing faster.
So the answer is 24 × 10³. But the rule says the front number must be at least 1 and less than 10. 24 is too big.
Slide the decimal point one place left: 24 becomes 2.4. You divided the front by 10, so multiply the back by 10 to keep things equal: 10³ becomes 10⁴.
Final answer: 2.4 × 10⁴, which is 24,000.

practice.stem: Which expression equals 2⁵ × 2³?
practice.explain: Same base, multiplying → add the powers: 2⁵⁺³ = 2⁸. 2¹⁵ multiplies the powers; 4⁸ and 4¹⁵ wrongly multiply the bases too.

practice.stem: Write 0.00047 in scientific notation.
practice.explain: Move the point 4 places right to get 4.7. A small number (under 1) gets a negative power: 4.7 × 10⁻⁴. 4.7 × 10⁴ is 47,000 — a big number.

practice.stem: Simplify √50 + √18.
practice.explain: √50 = √(25 × 2) = 5√2 and √18 = √(9 × 2) = 3√2. Like roots add: 8√2. √68 adds under the root (not allowed); 34√2 pulls out 25 and 9 instead of their roots 5 and 3.

practice.stem: Evaluate 4⁻² × 8.
practice.explain: 4⁻² = 1/4² = 1/16. Then 1/16 × 8 = 8/16 = 1/2. −128 treats the negative power as a negative number.

practice.stem: What is (3.2 × 10⁶) ÷ (8 × 10⁻³) in scientific notation?
practice.explain: Fronts: 3.2 ÷ 8 = 0.4. Powers: 10⁶ ÷ 10⁻³ = 10⁹ (subtract: 6 − (−3) = 9). So 0.4 × 10⁹ = 4 × 10⁸. 4 × 10² subtracts 3 instead of −3; 4 × 10⁹ forgets to adjust the power when 0.4 becomes 4; 2.5 divides 8 by 3.2.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's write the powers out longhand so the rules explain themselves.
steps: x³ · x² = (x·x·x)(x·x) = five x's = x⁵. Counting the x's is why you ADD powers when multiplying.
x⁵ ÷ x² = (x·x·x·x·x) ÷ (x·x): two pairs cancel, three x's are left = x³. That's why you SUBTRACT when dividing.
Keep dividing: x² ÷ x² = 1, so x⁰ = 1. One more: x² ÷ x³ = 1/x, so x⁻¹ = 1/x. Negative powers mean 'one over'.
(x²)³ means x² three times: x² · x² · x² = x⁶. Power of a power → MULTIPLY.
Roots: look for the biggest perfect square inside. √48 = √16 × √3 = 4√3.
Multiply same base → add powers
Divide → subtract powers
Bracket power → multiply powers
Negative power → one over

example.stem: Simplify (2³)² ÷ 2⁴.
steps: (2³)² = 2⁶ — bracket power, so multiply 3 × 2.
2⁶ ÷ 2⁴ = 2² — dividing, so subtract 6 − 4.
Longhand check: 8² = 64, and 64 ÷ 16 = 4 ✓.

reteach.hook: Times → add. Divide → subtract. Bracket → multiply.

check.stem: Simplify x⁷ · x⁻³.
check.explain: Multiplying, so add the powers: 7 + (−3) = 4, giving x⁴. x¹⁰ ignores the minus sign; x⁻²¹ multiplies the powers.

check.stem: Simplify √75.
check.explain: 75 = 25 × 3, and √25 = 5, so √75 = 5√3. 25√3 pulls out 25 instead of its root, 5.

check.stem: What is (5 × 10³) × (6 × 10⁴) in scientific notation?
check.explain: 5 × 6 = 30 and 10³ × 10⁴ = 10⁷, giving 30 × 10⁷ = 3 × 10⁸. 3 × 10⁷ shrinks 30 to 3 without raising the power; 3 × 10¹² multiplies the powers; 1.1 adds 5 and 6.

check.stem: What is the value of 2⁻³?
check.explain: A negative power means one over: 2⁻³ = 1/2³ = 1/8. It is not negative, and it is not 2 × −3.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: An exponent counts how many times a number is multiplied by itself: 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16.
The big number is the base. The small raised number is the exponent, or power.
A square root undoes squaring: √49 = 7, because 7 × 7 = 49.
Multiplying the same base: add the powers. 3² × 3³ = 3⁵.
Dividing the same base: subtract the powers. 3⁵ ÷ 3² = 3³.
Any number to the power 0 is 1. 7⁰ = 1.
Scientific notation writes a number as (a number from 1 to 9.99…) × 10 to a power.
The power of 10 counts how many places the decimal point moved: 3,000 = 3 × 10³.

example.stem: Write 52,000 in scientific notation.
steps: Put the decimal point after the first digit: 5.2.
Count how far the point moved from 52,000. to 5.2: 4 places.
It's a big number, so the power is positive: 5.2 × 10⁴.

reteach.hook: Same base: times → add, divide → subtract.

check.stem: What is 3⁴?
check.explain: 3 × 3 × 3 × 3 = 81. 12 is 3 × 4, which is not what a power means.

check.stem: What is √144?
check.explain: 12 × 12 = 144, so √144 = 12. 72 is half of 144, not its square root.

check.stem: Simplify 4² × 4³.
check.explain: Same base, multiplying → add the powers: 2 + 3 = 5, so 4⁵. 4⁶ multiplies the powers; 16⁵ multiplies the bases.

check.stem: Write 7,300,000 in scientific notation.
check.explain: Moving the point from 7,300,000. to 7.3 is 6 places, and it's a big number, so 7.3 × 10⁶.

units.title: Geometry: angles, area, volume & Pythagoras
units.objective: Combine angle facts, shape formulas and the Pythagorean theorem in one multi-step problem.

steps: Angles: a straight line = 180°, a triangle's angles total 180°, a four-sided shape's total 360°, a full turn = 360°.
Area: rectangle l × w; triangle ½ × base × height; circle πr²; trapezoid ½(b₁ + b₂) × h. Circumference = 2πr = πd.
Volume: box l × w × h; cylinder πr²h. Scale every length by k and area scales by k², volume by k³.
Pythagoras (right triangles only): a² + b² = c². Learn the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and their multiples (6-8-10, 10-24-26).
Composite shapes: split into simple pieces and add, or take the big shape and subtract the hole. Always check radius vs diameter.
teach.formula: a² + b² = c²   ·   cylinder volume = πr²h

worked.stem: A rectangular panel 24 ft long and 10 ft wide is cut along its diagonal into two triangles. What is the perimeter of one triangle?
steps: Each triangle has the two panel sides (24 and 10) plus the diagonal.
The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle: 24² + 10² = 576 + 100 = 676.
√676 = 26 (it's the 5-12-13 triple doubled: 10-24-26).
Perimeter = 24 + 10 + 26 = 60.
worked.answer: 60 ft

visual.caption: 10² + 24² = 676, so the diagonal is 26

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Draw it. A rectangle 24 long and 10 wide. Draw a line from one corner to the opposite corner. You now have two identical triangles.
Perimeter means the distance all the way around ONE triangle: two of its sides are the rectangle's sides (24 and 10). The third is that slanted line.
The rectangle's corner is a perfect right angle, so the slanted line is the long side of a right triangle. That's a Pythagoras job.
Square the two short sides: 24 × 24 = 576 and 10 × 10 = 100. Add them: 676.
Now ask: what number times itself is 676? 26 × 26 = 676. So the slanted side is 26.
Add the three sides: 24 + 10 + 26 = 60 feet. Perimeter is a plain length, so the unit is feet, not square feet.

practice.stem: Two angles of a triangle measure 47° and 68°. What is the third angle?
practice.explain: 180 − 47 − 68 = 65°. 115° is the two given angles added; 245° uses 360° instead of 180°.

practice.stem: A circular hatch has a diameter of 10 cm. What is its area? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
practice.explain: Radius = 10 ÷ 2 = 5. Area = 3.14 × 5² = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 cm². 314 squares the diameter; 31.4 is the circumference.

practice.stem: A cylindrical fuel drum has a radius of 2 ft and a height of 5 ft. What is its volume?
practice.explain: V = πr²h = π × 2² × 5 = 20π ft³. 80π uses the diameter (4) as the radius; 50π swaps the radius and height.

practice.stem: An aircraft flies 8 km due east, then 15 km due north. How far is it, in a straight line, from where it started?
practice.explain: The legs meet at a right angle: 8² + 15² = 64 + 225 = 289, and √289 = 17 km (the 8-15-17 triple). 23 is the distance flown; 289 forgets the square root.

practice.stem: A circle with a diameter of 10 in is cut out of a square sheet with sides of 10 in. What area of the sheet is left? (Use π ≈ 3.14.)
practice.explain: Square = 10 × 10 = 100. Circle: radius 5, area 3.14 × 25 = 78.5. Left over = 100 − 78.5 = 21.5 in². 68.6 subtracts the circumference (31.4); 84.3 subtracts π × 5 instead of π × 5².

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's sketch it, label it and break it into pieces you already know.
steps: Always sketch the shape and write every number on it. Most geometry mistakes are radius-vs-diameter or using the wrong side.
Composite shapes: big shape minus the hole, or add up simple pieces.
Unknown angles: write each angle in terms of x, set the total to 180° (triangle) or 360° (four sides), then solve.
Pythagoras triples save time: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17 and any multiple, such as 10-24-26 or 16-30-34.
Scaling: double every length → area × 4, volume × 8.

example.stem: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of 26 and one leg of 10. What is its area?
steps: Area needs both legs (base and height), so find the missing leg first.

reteach.hook: Sketch it, label it, find what's missing, then use the formula.

check.stem: In a triangle, angle B is twice angle A, and angle C is 20° more than angle A. What is angle B?
Every edge of a cube is doubled. Its volume is multiplied by —
check.explain: Volume scales by the cube of the length factor: 2³ = 8. 4 is how the AREA of each face changes.

check.stem: A rectangular field is 30 m by 16 m. How long is its diagonal?
check.explain: 30² + 16² = 900 + 256 = 1,156, and √1,156 = 34 (8-15-17 doubled). 46 adds the sides; 14 subtracts them.

check.stem: A circular helipad of radius 7 m sits on a square pad 20 m × 20 m. What area of the square is NOT covered? (Use π ≈ 22/7.)
check.explain: Square = 400. Circle = 22/7 × 7² = 22/7 × 49 = 154. Uncovered = 400 − 154 = 246 m². 356 subtracts the circumference (44); 154 is the circle itself.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Perimeter is the distance around a shape. Add up all the sides.
Area is the flat space inside. It's measured in square units, like ft².
Rectangle area = length × width.
Triangle area = half of base × height.
A circle's radius goes from the center to the edge. The diameter goes edge to edge and is twice the radius.
Circle area = π × radius × radius.
Volume is the space inside a solid. Box volume = length × width × height.
The three angles in any triangle add up to 180°.

example.stem: A triangle has a base of 12 cm and a height of 7 cm. What is its area?
steps: Base × height = 12 × 7 = 84.
Half of that: 84 ÷ 2 = 42.
Area is in square units: cm².

reteach.hook: Around = add the sides. Inside = use the area formula.

check.stem: A rectangle is 9 units long and 4 units wide. What is its perimeter?
check.explain: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26. 36 is the area; 13 only adds two sides.

check.stem: A circle has a radius of 3. What is its area?
check.explain: π × 3 × 3 = 9π. 6π is the circumference; 36π uses the diameter (6) as the radius.

check.stem: A box is 5 ft long, 4 ft wide and 3 ft high. What is its volume?
check.explain: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 ft³. 12 adds the edges; 94 is the surface area.

check.stem: Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 35°. What is the third angle?
check.explain: 180 − 90 − 35 = 55°. 125° is the two angles added.

units.title: Multi-step word problems: mixtures, averages & probability
units.objective: Break a long word problem into steps and use totals, conserved quantities and fractions to solve it.

steps: Read the LAST sentence first so you know what you're finding. Then list what you have, with units, and name the unknown x.
Mixtures: the pure ingredient is conserved. (strength × amount) + (strength × amount) = final strength × total amount.
Averages: work in TOTALS. Total = average × count. Totals add and subtract; averages don't.
Probability = favorable ÷ total. 'Both' or 'in a row' → multiply. Without replacement, the second draw has one fewer on top and bottom.
Sense-check: a mixture's strength lies between its two ingredients, and a probability is always between 0 and 1.
teach.formula: total = average × count

worked.stem: A pilot's first four checkride scores average 82. What score on the fifth checkride would bring the average up to exactly 85?
steps: Want: the fifth score, x.
Total so far = 82 × 4 = 328.
Total needed for an 85 average over 5 rides = 85 × 5 = 425.
Sense-check: each of the 4 earlier rides is 3 points short of 85, a 12-point gap. The fifth ride must hit 85 AND cover that gap: 85 + 12 = 97 ✓.

visual.caption: Four 82s plus a 97 total 425 — exactly 85 each when levelled out

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Averages are hard to work with directly, so turn them into totals. An average of 82 over 4 rides means the 4 scores add up to 82 × 4 = 328 points.
The goal is an average of 85 over 5 rides. That means the 5 scores must add up to 85 × 5 = 425 points.
You already have 328 points. How many more do you need to reach 425?
425 − 328 = 97. That's the score the fifth ride must earn.
Does it make sense? 97 is well above 85 — it has to be, to drag four 82s up to an 85 average.
The same 'totals' trick solves mixtures too: track the amount of pure stuff, which never changes when you pour things together.

practice.stem: A crew's five practice run times average 14 minutes. What is the total of the five times?
practice.explain: Total = average × count = 14 × 5 = 70 minutes. 2.8 divides instead of multiplying.

practice.stem: A box holds 3 red, 5 blue and 4 green fuses. One is drawn at random. What is the probability it is blue?
practice.explain: Total fuses = 3 + 5 + 4 = 12; blue = 5, so 5/12. 7/12 is the chance of NOT blue; 5/7 compares blue with non-blue (a ratio, not a probability); 1/3 assumes each color is equally likely.

practice.stem: How many liters of 80% antifreeze must be added to 10 L of 20% antifreeze to make a 40% mixture?
A tray holds 5 good relays and 3 faulty ones. Two are taken at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are faulty?
practice.explain: First faulty: 3/8. Then 2 faulty left out of 7: 2/7. Both: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28. 9/64 assumes the first relay is put back; 3/32 takes one away on top but not underneath; 5/14 is both GOOD.

practice.stem: The average fitness score of 12 soldiers is 78. After 3 new soldiers join, the average of all 15 is 80. What is the average score of the 3 newcomers?
practice.explain: Old total = 12 × 78 = 936. New total = 15 × 80 = 1,200. Newcomers' total = 1,200 − 936 = 264, so their average = 264 ÷ 3 = 88. 264 is their total, not their average; 82 just nudges the average.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Long problems are just short ones glued together — let's take them apart.
steps: Underline the question at the END first, so you know exactly what you're hunting for.
Mixtures: make a table with three rows (first liquid, second liquid, final mix) and columns amount × strength = pure stuff. The pure-stuff column adds up.
Averages: switch to totals. Totals add and subtract; averages don't.
Probability of 'both' or 'two in a row': multiply. Without replacement, take one away from the top AND bottom for the second draw.
Finish with a sense-check: between the two strengths? Under 1 for a probability?
Underline the question
List what you know
Pick the tool: table, totals or fractions
Solve, then sense-check

example.stem: How many liters of water must be added to 12 L of a 50% solution to dilute it to 30%?
steps: Pure stuff now: 50% of 12 = 6 L. Adding water doesn't change it.
At 30%, those 6 L must be 30% of the new total: total = 6 ÷ 0.30 = 20 L.
Water added = 20 − 12 = 8 L.
Sense-check: 6 L in 20 L = 30% ✓.

reteach.hook: Track what doesn't change: the pure stuff, or the total.

check.stem: The mean of 6 numbers is 15. One number is removed, and the mean of the other 5 is 14. What number was removed?
check.explain: Totals: 6 × 15 = 90 and 5 × 14 = 70. Removed = 90 − 70 = 20. 1 just subtracts the averages.

check.stem: A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue tokens. Two are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are blue?
check.explain: 6/10 × 5/9 = 30/90 = 1/3. 9/25 puts the first token back; 2/15 is both RED.

check.stem: 4 L of a 25% solution is mixed with 6 L of a 50% solution. What is the strength of the mixture?
check.explain: Pure stuff: 1 L + 3 L = 4 L in 10 L total = 40%. 37.5% averages the two strengths, ignoring that there's more of the 50% one.

check.stem: A 400-gallon tank is 3/8 full. A pump adds 25 gallons per minute. How many minutes until it is 7/8 full?
check.explain: Needed: 7/8 − 3/8 = 4/8 = 1/2 of 400 = 200 gallons. 200 ÷ 25 = 8 minutes. 14 fills to 7/8 from empty; 16 fills the whole tank.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Read the LAST sentence first. That's what you are finding.
Write down every number with its label, like '12 L' or '50%'.
Average = total ÷ how many.
So total = average × how many.
Probability = the ways you want ÷ all the ways there are.
A probability is always between 0 and 1.
For a mixture, find the amount of pure stuff: percent × amount.
Do one small step at a time and write each answer down.

example.stem: Three scores are 10, 14 and 18. What is their average?
steps: Count them: 3 scores.
Divide: 42 ÷ 3 = 14.

reteach.hook: Average = total ÷ count. Total = average × count.

check.stem: What is the average of 8, 12, 13 and 15?
check.explain: 8 + 12 + 13 + 15 = 48, and 48 ÷ 4 = 12. 48 is the total, not the average.

check.stem: Four numbers have an average of 20. What is their total?
check.explain: Total = average × count = 20 × 4 = 80. 5 divides instead of multiplying.

check.stem: A drawer has 2 black socks and 8 white socks. One is picked at random. What is the probability it is black?
check.explain: 2 black out of 10 socks = 2/10 = 1/5. 1/4 compares black with white (2 to 8) instead of with all the socks; 4/5 is white.

check.stem: How many liters of pure acid are in 20 L of a 15% acid solution?
check.explain: 15% of 20 = 0.15 × 20 = 3 L. 17 L is the water, not the acid.

sift-mechanical.title: Mechanical Comprehension
sift-mechanical.blurb: SIFT-level mechanics: torque and balance, gear and pulley trade-offs, work, energy and power, and the fluid physics behind hydraulics and lift. Expect real calculations.

units.title: Levers, torque & balance
units.objective: Add up turning effects (moments) to balance levers, find forces and locate a center of gravity.

steps: Torque (also called a moment) is a turning effect: torque = force × lever arm, where the lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force. Units: lb-ft or N·m.
An object is in equilibrium when two things are true: the forces cancel (no net push) AND the torques cancel (no net turn). So total clockwise torque = total counterclockwise torque.
With several weights on one side, work out each weight × its distance, then add them. Compare the totals on each side, not the individual weights.
For a lever balanced on a pivot with only vertical loads, the pivot pushes up with a force equal to all the downward loads added together.

Ideal mechanical advantage of a lever = effort arm ÷ load arm. A wheelbarrow (load in the middle) has MA above 1; your forearm (effort in the middle) has MA below 1, trading force for speed and range of motion.
Aircraft weight and balance uses the same sum: each weight × its arm from a reference line (the datum) gives a moment, and center of gravity = total moment ÷ total weight.
teach.formula: clockwise moments = counterclockwise moments  (F₁ × d₁ = F₂ × d₂)

visual.caption: 150 × 2 = 300 lb-ft each way, so the bar balances.

worked.stem: A light beam is pivoted at its center. A 120 lb weight sits 3 ft left of the pivot and a 40 lb weight sits 6 ft right of it. Where on the right must a 60 lb weight go to balance the beam, and what force does the pivot carry?
steps: Left (counterclockwise) moment: 120 × 3 = 360 lb-ft.
Right side already has 40 × 6 = 240 lb-ft, so it still needs 360 − 240 = 120 lb-ft.
60 lb × d = 120 lb-ft, so d = 2 ft right of the pivot.
Check: 240 + 60 × 2 = 360 lb-ft on the right. Balanced.
Pivot force = all the downward loads: 120 + 40 + 60 = 220 lb.
worked.answer: 2 ft right of the pivot; the pivot carries 220 lb

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of a wrench on a stuck bolt. Push harder, or push further out along the handle, and the bolt turns more easily.
That 'turning power' is torque. Work it out by multiplying: how hard you push × how far from the pivot you push.
A seesaw balances when the turning power trying to drop the left side equals the turning power trying to drop the right side.
In the worked example the left side's turning power is 120 × 3 = 360.
The right side has 40 × 6 = 240 already. It is 120 short.
The 60 lb weight has to supply that missing 120: 60 × 2 = 120, so it goes 2 ft out.
The pivot is holding the whole lot up, so it carries every weight added together: 120 + 40 + 60 = 220 lb.

practice.stem: A mechanic pushes at right angles on a wrench handle with 50 N, 0.4 m from the center of the bolt. What torque does she apply?
practice.explain: Torque = force × lever arm = 50 × 0.4 = 20 N·m. 125 N·m comes from dividing 50 by 0.4 instead of multiplying.

practice.stem: What weight on the right balances this lever?
practice.explain: Left moment = 80 × 3 = 240 lb-ft. Right: ? × 4 = 240, so ? = 60 lb. 106.7 lb comes from flipping the distances; 240 lb is the moment, not the weight.

practice.stem: The wheelbarrow carries 200 lb whose weight acts 1.5 ft from the wheel axle (the fulcrum). The handles are 5 ft from the axle. What upward force F at the handles holds it level?
practice.explain: F × 5 = 200 × 1.5 = 300 lb-ft, so F = 60 lb. 667 lb flips the distances; 40 lb divides by 5 without using the 1.5 ft arm; 300 lb is the moment.

practice.stem: Your forearm is a lever pivoting at the elbow. The biceps attaches 2 in from the elbow, and your hand holds a 10 lb weight 14 in from the elbow. Ignoring the arm's own weight, what force must the biceps supply to hold the forearm level?
practice.explain: Biceps × 2 = 10 × 14 = 140 lb-in, so the biceps pulls 70 lb. This is a third-class lever (effort between pivot and load) with MA = 2 ÷ 14 below 1: big force in, but the hand moves fast and far. 1.4 lb flips the arms; 140 lb is the moment.

practice.stem: An aircraft's empty weight is 1,500 lb with its center of gravity 40 in aft of the datum. A 200 lb pilot sits 35 in aft of the datum and 300 lb of fuel is 50 in aft. Where is the loaded center of gravity?
practice.explain: Moments: 1,500 × 40 = 60,000; 200 × 35 = 7,000; 300 × 50 = 15,000. Total 82,000 lb-in ÷ total weight 2,000 lb = 41.0 in. 41.7 in averages the three arms (or drops the pilot); 39.4 in leaves out the fuel.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's treat torque as a turning score and keep a tally for each direction.
steps: Every weight or push on a lever gets a turning score: force × distance from the pivot.
Sort the scores into two piles: the ones trying to turn the bar clockwise, and the ones trying to turn it counterclockwise.
Add each pile. If the two totals match, the bar balances. If not, the bigger pile wins and the bar tips that way.
To find a missing force or distance, work out how much the short pile is missing, then divide by the number you do know.
The pivot holds everything up, so its upward push is just all the downward forces added together.

visual.caption: 90 × 4 = 360 and 120 × 3 = 360. Equal scores, so it balances.

example.stem: A bolt needs 60 lb-ft of torque to loosen. Your wrench is 1.5 ft long and you push at the very end, at right angles. What force do you need?
steps: Torque = force × distance, so 60 = F × 1.5.
Check: 40 × 1.5 = 60 lb-ft.

reteach.hook: Add the turning scores on each side. Equal totals = balance.

check.stem: What weight on the right balances this lever?
check.explain: Left score = 75 × 4 = 300 lb-ft. ? × 5 = 300, so ? = 60 lb. 93.75 lb comes from flipping the distances; 300 lb is the score, not the weight.

check.stem: A nut must be tightened to 90 N·m. The mechanic pushes at right angles 0.3 m from the nut's center. What force is needed?
check.explain: F × 0.3 = 90, so F = 90 ÷ 0.3 = 300 N. 27 N multiplies 90 × 0.3 instead of dividing; 30 N and 3,000 N are decimal slips.

check.stem: A light 16 ft plank pivots at its center. A 90 lb weight sits 4 ft left of the pivot and a 30 lb weight sits 2 ft right of it. How far right of the pivot must a 60 lb weight go to balance the plank?
check.explain: Left: 90 × 4 = 360 lb-ft. Right already has 30 × 2 = 60, so it needs 300 more: 300 ÷ 60 = 5 ft. 6 ft forgets the 30 lb weight; 7 ft adds its score to the wrong side.

check.stem: A 200 lb load 2 ft left of a pivot balances a 100 lb load 4 ft right of it on a light bar. What upward force does the pivot provide?
check.explain: The pivot carries everything pressing down: 200 + 100 = 300 lb. 800 lb adds the two turning scores (400 + 400), which are not forces.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Torque is a turning push, like using a wrench on a bolt.
It depends on two things: how hard you push, and how far from the pivot you push.
Torque = force × distance from the pivot.
Push 20 lb, 2 ft from a bolt: 20 × 2 = 40 lb-ft.
Push the same 20 lb, 4 ft away: 20 × 4 = 80 lb-ft. Twice the turn.
A seesaw balances when the left side's torque equals the right side's torque.
20 lb at 4 ft makes 80. 40 lb at 2 ft also makes 80. So they balance.

visual.caption: 20 × 4 = 80 and 40 × 2 = 80. Balanced.

example.stem: 30 lb sits 2 ft left of the pivot. What weight 3 ft right of the pivot balances it?
steps: Left torque: 30 × 2 = 60.
The right side must also make 60.

reteach.hook: Torque = force × distance. Left torque = right torque.

check.stem: You push with 10 lb at right angles to a wrench, 3 ft from the bolt. What torque do you apply?
check.explain: Torque = force × distance = 10 × 3 = 30 lb-ft. 13 lb-ft adds the numbers; 3.3 lb-ft divides them.

check.stem: What weight on the right balances this lever?
check.explain: 60 × 2 = 120, and ? × 4 = 120, so ? = 30 lb. The right weight is twice as far out, so it only needs to be half as heavy.

check.stem: To loosen a stuck nut with less force, you should —
options: grip the wrench closer to the nut
use a longer wrench and push near the end
push along the handle toward the nut
check.explain: More distance from the pivot gives more torque for the same force. Pushing along the handle toward the nut has no turning effect at all.

check.stem: A crowbar's fulcrum is 3 in from the load and 30 in from where you push. What is its ideal mechanical advantage?
check.explain: Ideal MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 30 ÷ 3 = 10, so every 1 lb of push makes 10 lb at the load. 90 multiplies the arms; 27 and 33 subtract and add them.

units.title: Pulleys, gears & belts
units.objective: Calculate speed, torque, effort and direction through pulley systems, gear trains and belt drives.

steps: Pulley systems: ideal mechanical advantage = the number of rope strands holding up the moving block. Effort = load ÷ strands, but you pull strands × as much rope as the load rises.
Meshed gears pass the same number of teeth per minute, so teeth × rpm is the same for both: rpm(out) = rpm(in) × teeth(in) ÷ teeth(out).
Torque goes the other way: torque(out) = torque(in) × teeth(out) ÷ teeth(in). Ideally torque × rpm (that is, power) is unchanged; a gearbox trades speed for twist, never creates energy.
Each mesh reverses direction. An idler gear between two others changes neither speed ratio nor torque ratio of the outer pair, but makes the last gear turn the same way as the first.
In a compound train (two gears fixed on one shaft), multiply the stage ratios: a 3 : 1 stage followed by another 3 : 1 stage gives 9 : 1.

Belts: rim speed is shared, so diameter × rpm is the same on both pulleys. An open belt keeps the direction; a crossed belt reverses it. A piston aircraft's propeller reduction gearbox is the same trade: the prop turns slower than the crankshaft but with more torque.
teach.formula: teeth_A × rpm_A = teeth_B × rpm_B ;  torque_B = torque_A × (teeth_B ÷ teeth_A)

visual.caption: 20 × 3,000 = 60,000 teeth a minute, so B turns 60,000 ÷ 50 = 1,200 rpm.

worked.stem: An engine turns a 20-tooth gear at 3,000 rpm with 100 lb-ft of torque. It meshes with a 50-tooth gear on the propeller shaft. Ignoring losses, find the propeller's rpm, its torque and its direction.
steps: Check power: 100 × 3,000 = 300,000 and 250 × 1,200 = 300,000. Equal, as they must be.
One mesh, so the propeller turns the opposite way to the engine gear.
worked.answer: 1,200 rpm, 250 lb-ft, opposite direction

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture the two gears as one tooth pushing one tooth. Every tooth on the small gear that goes past the contact point pushes one tooth on the big gear past it too.
In one minute the 20-tooth gear turns 3,000 times, so 20 × 3,000 = 60,000 teeth go past.
The big gear also has 60,000 teeth go past. With 50 teeth per turn, that is 60,000 ÷ 50 = 1,200 turns. Slower.
A machine never gives something for nothing. The big gear turns 2.5 times slower, so it twists 2.5 times harder: 100 × 2.5 = 250 lb-ft.
Two meshed gears always turn opposite ways, like two hands rubbing past each other.
Summary: the bigger gear is slower and stronger; the smaller gear is faster and weaker.

practice.stem: The load in this block and tackle weighs 240 lb. Ignoring friction and the pulleys' weight, what effort F is needed to hold it?
practice.explain: Four strands support the load, so each carries 240 ÷ 4 = 60 lb, and that is the pull on the free end. 80 lb counts only three strands; 960 lb multiplies instead of dividing.

practice.stem: Gear A turns at 90 rpm. How fast does gear B turn?
practice.explain: 12 × 90 = 1,080 teeth per minute; 1,080 ÷ 36 = 30 rpm. The bigger gear turns slower, so 270 rpm (multiplying by 3) is backwards.

practice.stem: An open belt connects pulley A (4 in diameter, 500 rpm) to pulley B (10 in diameter). What does pulley B do?
practice.explain: Diameter × rpm is shared: 4 × 500 = 2,000, so B turns 2,000 ÷ 10 = 200 rpm. An open (uncrossed) belt keeps the same direction; only a crossed belt reverses it.

practice.stem: In this gear train, A turns clockwise at 120 rpm. What does gear C do?
practice.explain: B is an idler: A to C is simply 15 → 30 teeth, so C = 120 × 15 ÷ 30 = 60 rpm. Two meshes reverse twice, so C turns the same way as A: clockwise. 40 rpm is B's speed, not C's.

practice.stem: A motor delivers 10 N·m at 1,800 rpm to a 12-tooth gear driving a 36-tooth gear. A 15-tooth gear fixed on the same shaft as the 36-tooth gear drives a 45-tooth output gear. Ignoring losses, what are the output speed and torque?
practice.explain: Each stage is 3 : 1 (36 ÷ 12 and 45 ÷ 15), and compound stages multiply: 3 × 3 = 9. Speed 1,800 ÷ 9 = 200 rpm; torque 10 × 9 = 90 N·m. 600 rpm / 30 N·m stops after one stage; 300 rpm / 60 N·m adds the ratios instead of multiplying.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's just count teeth, turns and rope strands.
steps: Where two gears touch, one tooth pushes one tooth. So both gears pass the same number of teeth every minute: teeth × rpm is equal on both.
Divide that shared number by a gear's teeth to get its rpm. Fewer teeth = faster spin.
Torque does the opposite: the slower gear twists harder by the same factor.
Direction: every mesh flips it. Count the meshes: odd number = opposite to the driver, even = same as the driver.
Belts share rim speed, so diameter × rpm is equal. Open belt keeps direction; crossed belt flips it.
Pulleys: count the strands holding the moving block. Effort = load ÷ strands; rope pulled = lift × strands.

example.stem: A 16-tooth gear turning at 600 rpm drives a 48-tooth gear. How fast does the big gear turn, and how does its torque compare?
steps: Teeth per minute: 16 × 600 = 9,600.
Big gear: 9,600 ÷ 48 = 200 rpm (3 times slower).
So its torque is 3 times larger, and it turns the opposite way.
example.answer: 200 rpm, 3 times the torque, opposite direction

reteach.hook: Teeth × rpm is shared. Slower gear = stronger gear.

check.stem: Gear A turns at 200 rpm. How fast does gear B turn?
check.explain: 40 × 200 = 8,000 teeth a minute; 8,000 ÷ 16 = 500 rpm. B is the smaller gear, so it must spin faster; 80 rpm has the ratio upside down.

check.stem: Ignoring friction, what effort F holds this 450 lb load, and how much rope must be pulled to raise the load 2 ft?
check.explain: Three strands share the load: 450 ÷ 3 = 150 lb. The trade is distance: 2 ft × 3 = 6 ft of rope. 150 lb; 2 ft would mean getting something for nothing.

check.stem: Gear A turns clockwise at 300 rpm. What does gear C do?
check.explain: B is an idler, so C acts as if it meshed with A directly: same teeth (20), same speed, 300 rpm. Two meshes flip the direction twice, so C turns clockwise like A. 100 rpm is B's speed.

check.stem: A crossed belt connects a 6 in pulley turning clockwise at 400 rpm to a 16 in pulley. What does the 16 in pulley do?
check.explain: Diameter × rpm is shared: 6 × 400 = 2,400, and 2,400 ÷ 16 = 150 rpm. A crossed belt reverses direction, so it turns counterclockwise.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Gears are wheels with teeth that lock together.
When one gear turns clockwise, the gear it touches turns counterclockwise.
Each tooth on gear A pushes one tooth on gear B.
A 10-tooth gear turning once pushes 10 teeth past the contact point.
A 20-tooth gear needs 20 teeth to go round once. With only 10 pushed, it goes halfway round.
So the big gear turns more slowly than the small one.
In return, the big gear twists harder: more torque.
Small gear: fast and weak. Big gear: slow and strong.

visual.caption: A turns twice for every one turn of B, so B turns at 50 rpm.

example.stem: A 12-tooth gear makes 4 full turns. How many turns does the 24-tooth gear it meshes with make?
steps: Teeth pushed past: 12 × 4 = 48.
The big gear needs 24 teeth per turn.

reteach.hook: Big gear = slow and strong. Small gear = fast and weak.

check.stem: Gear A turns clockwise and meshes directly with gear B. Which way does B turn?
options: it depends on which gear is bigger
check.explain: Directly meshed gears always turn opposite ways, whatever their sizes. Size changes the speed, never the direction.

check.stem: Gear A turns at 90 rpm. How fast does gear B turn?
check.explain: B has 3 times as many teeth, so it turns 3 times slower: 90 ÷ 3 = 30 rpm. 270 rpm multiplies instead of dividing.

check.stem: A 15-tooth gear meshes with a 45-tooth gear. Which one turns with more torque?
options: both turn with the same torque
check.explain: The bigger gear turns 3 times slower, so it twists 3 times harder. Torque goes up as speed goes down.

check.stem: Ignoring friction, what effort F holds this 160 lb load?
check.explain: Two strands hold the load, so each carries half: 160 ÷ 2 = 80 lb. 40 lb would need four strands.

units.title: Work, energy, power & ramps
units.objective: Use work, energy conservation and power to solve inclined-plane, screw and climb problems.

steps: Work = force × distance moved in the direction of the force (ft-lb or joules). If nothing moves, or the motion is at right angles to the force, that force does no work.

Energy is stored work. Potential energy = weight × height (mgh in SI). Kinetic energy = ½mv². Without friction or drag, one converts into the other: a falling object reaches v = √(2gh), and a coasting climb gains h = v² ÷ 2g.
Power = work ÷ time. 1 horsepower = 550 ft-lb per second ≈ 746 W.
The golden rule of machines: ideal work in = work out. For a ramp, effort × ramp length = load × height, so ideal MA = length ÷ height. A longer, gentler ramp needs less force over more distance.
A screw is a ramp wrapped around a cylinder. One turn of a handle of radius r moves your hand 2πr while the load rises one pitch, so ideal MA = 2πr ÷ pitch.
Real machines lose some work to friction. Efficiency = useful work out ÷ work in (or actual MA ÷ ideal MA), always under 100%.
teach.formula: work = force × distance;  power = work ÷ time;  ideal: effort × effort distance = load × load distance

visual.caption: Ideal MA = 12 ÷ 3 = 4: a quarter of the force, over four times the distance.

worked.stem: A 600 lb crate is pushed up a frictionless 12 ft ramp onto a platform 3 ft high, taking 6 seconds. What push is needed, how much work is done and what is the average power?
steps: Work to raise the crate: 600 × 3 = 1,800 ft-lb.
The same 1,800 ft-lb is spread over the 12 ft ramp: 1,800 ÷ 12 = 150 lb push.
Check: 150 lb × 12 ft = 1,800 ft-lb. Same work either way.
worked.answer: 150 lb push, 1,800 ft-lb of work, 300 ft-lb/s (about 0.55 hp)

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Work is the 'effort bill' for moving something: how hard you push × how far it moves.
Lifting the 600 lb crate straight up 3 ft costs 600 × 3 = 1,800 ft-lb. That bill has to be paid whichever way you get it there.
A ramp doesn't make the bill smaller. It lets you pay it in smaller pieces over a longer distance.
The ramp is 12 ft long, so share the 1,800 out over 12 ft: 1,800 ÷ 12 = 150 lb of push.
Power is how quickly you pay the bill. 1,800 ft-lb in 6 seconds is 1,800 ÷ 6 = 300 ft-lb every second.
One horsepower is 550 ft-lb every second, so 300 is a bit over half a horsepower.

practice.stem: How much work is done lifting a 50 lb ammunition box straight up onto a shelf 4 ft higher?
practice.explain: Work = force × distance = 50 × 4 = 200 ft-lb. 12.5 ft-lb divides instead of multiplying; 54 ft-lb adds; 100 ft-lb wrongly halves it.

practice.stem: Ignoring friction, what force pushed along this ramp moves a 400 lb load up it?
practice.explain: Effort × length = load × height: F × 15 = 400 × 3 = 1,200, so F = 80 lb. 133 lb divides by the height only; 2,000 lb flips the ratio.

practice.stem: A winch lifts a 1,100 lb engine 20 ft in 10 seconds. What is its average power output? (1 hp = 550 ft-lb/s)
practice.explain: Work = 1,100 × 20 = 22,000 ft-lb. Power = 22,000 ÷ 10 = 2,200 ft-lb/s, and 2,200 ÷ 550 = 4 hp. 40 hp forgets to divide by the time.

practice.stem: An aircraft at 60 m/s pulls up into a climb with the engine at idle. Ignoring drag and taking g = 10 m/s², how much height can it gain by trading all its speed for altitude?
practice.explain: Kinetic energy becomes potential energy: ½mv² = mgh, so h = v² ÷ 2g = 3,600 ÷ 20 = 180 m. Mass cancels. 360 m forgets the ½; 6 m is just v ÷ g.

practice.stem: A screw jack has a handle 14 in long (the hand moves in a circle of 14 in radius) and a thread pitch of 0.25 in. Ignoring friction and taking π = 22/7, what handle force raises a 4,400 lb load?
practice.explain: One turn moves the hand 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 14 = 88 in while the load rises 0.25 in, so ideal MA = 88 ÷ 0.25 = 352. Force = 4,400 ÷ 352 = 12.5 lb. 25 lb uses πr instead of 2πr; 78.6 lb leaves out the 2π; 50 lb forgets the pitch.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's follow the energy, because a machine can only move it around, never make more.
steps: Work is energy moved: force × distance. Lifting 100 lb by 2 ft stores 200 ft-lb of energy in the object, however you lift it.
A machine lets you choose how to pay: a big force over a short distance, or a small force over a long distance. The product stays the same.
Ramp: push × ramp length = weight × height. Screw: push × 2πr = load × pitch.
Falling or coasting swaps height for speed and back: weight × height ↔ ½mv².
Friction steals some work, so a real machine needs more push than the ideal answer. Efficiency = work out ÷ work in.
Power just adds a clock: work ÷ seconds. 550 ft-lb every second = 1 hp.

visual.caption: Raising a load 4 ft by pushing it along 20 ft: one fifth of the force.

example.stem: A 500 lb barrel is rolled up a frictionless 20 ft ramp onto a dock 4 ft high. What push is needed?
steps: Energy the barrel gains: 500 × 4 = 2,000 ft-lb.
Pay it over 20 ft of ramp: 2,000 ÷ 20 = 100 lb.

reteach.hook: Force × distance in = force × distance out. Machines trade, they don't create.

check.stem: Ignoring friction, what force pushed along this ramp moves a 350 lb cart up it?
check.explain: F × 10 = 350 × 2 = 700, so F = 70 lb. 175 lb divides by the height only; 35 lb divides by the length only; 1,750 lb flips the ratio.

check.stem: On a real 10 ft ramp, it takes a 100 lb push to move a 350 lb cart up 2 ft. What is the ramp's efficiency?
check.explain: Work out = 350 × 2 = 700 ft-lb. Work in = 100 × 10 = 1,000 ft-lb. Efficiency = 700 ÷ 1,000 = 70%. Anything over 100% would mean creating energy.

check.stem: A 2 kg wrench falls 5 m from a hangar gantry. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s², how much kinetic energy does it have just before it hits the floor?
check.explain: All the potential energy becomes kinetic: mgh = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. 10 J leaves out g; 50 J wrongly brings in a ½, which belongs to ½mv², not mgh.

check.stem: A 165 lb soldier climbs a 30 ft rope in 9 seconds. What is his average power output? (1 hp = 550 ft-lb/s)
check.explain: Work = 165 × 30 = 4,950 ft-lb. Power = 4,950 ÷ 9 = 550 ft-lb/s = 1 hp. 9 hp forgets to divide by the time.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Work means a force moving something.
Work = force × the distance it moves.
Lift a 10 lb bag up 3 ft: 10 × 3 = 30 ft-lb of work.
Hold the bag still and nothing moves, so no work is done on it.
A ramp lets you push with less force than lifting straight up.
But you have to push it a longer distance.
The work comes out the same: small force × long ramp = big weight × short height.
Power is how fast you do work: power = work ÷ time.

visual.caption: The ramp is 4 times longer than it is high, so you push with a quarter of the weight.

example.stem: A 100 lb box is pushed up a frictionless ramp 8 ft long and 2 ft high. What push is needed?
steps: Work to lift the box 2 ft: 100 × 2 = 200 ft-lb.
Spread that over the 8 ft ramp: 200 ÷ 8 = 25.
Check: 25 × 8 = 200 ft-lb.

reteach.hook: Work = force × distance. A ramp swaps less force for more distance.

check.stem: How much work is done lifting a 25 lb box 4 ft straight up?
check.explain: Work = force × distance = 25 × 4 = 100 ft-lb. 29 ft-lb adds the numbers; 6.25 ft-lb divides them.

check.stem: A soldier holds a 40 lb pack perfectly still at shoulder height for 2 minutes. How much work does he do on the pack?
check.explain: Work needs movement. The pack doesn't move, so no work is done on it, even though his muscles get tired.

check.stem: A machine does 600 J of work in 3 seconds. What is its power?
check.explain: Power = work ÷ time = 600 ÷ 3 = 200 W (joules per second). 1,800 W multiplies instead of dividing.

check.stem: Ignoring friction, what force pushed along this ramp moves an 80 lb box up it?
check.explain: Lifting work = 80 × 3 = 240 ft-lb. Over the 12 ft ramp: 240 ÷ 12 = 20 lb. 320 lb flips the ratio; 26.7 lb divides by the height only.

units.title: Fluids: hydraulics, Bernoulli & lift
units.objective: Use pressure, Pascal's principle and Bernoulli's principle to solve hydraulic problems and explain how a wing makes lift.

steps: Pressure = force ÷ area: psi (lb per square inch) or pascals (N per square meter). Pressure in a still liquid increases with depth (P = ρgh), and depends only on depth, not on the container's shape.
Pascal's principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid reaches every part of it undiminished. So F₁ ÷ A₁ = F₂ ÷ A₂, and the bigger piston gets the bigger force.

The trade-off: the fluid volume pushed out of the small cylinder equals the volume into the large one, so A₁ × d₁ = A₂ × d₂. Force up by 25 means travel down by 25. Area grows with diameter squared, so double the diameter = 4 × the area.
Continuity: a fluid flowing through a pipe keeps A × v constant, so it speeds up where the pipe narrows (a venturi).
Bernoulli's principle: where a moving fluid speeds up, its pressure drops. Faster flow, lower pressure.

Lift: the wing's shape and angle of attack make air flow faster over the top, so pressure on top is lower than underneath; lift = pressure difference × wing area. (The wing also deflects air downward; Bernoulli and Newton describe the same lift.) Lift grows with the square of airspeed: L = ½ρv² × wing area × lift coefficient.
teach.formula: P = F ÷ A;  F₁ ÷ A₁ = F₂ ÷ A₂;  A₁ × v₁ = A₂ × v₂;  faster flow → lower pressure

visual.caption: 40 lb ÷ 2 in² = 20 psi everywhere; 20 psi × 50 in² = 1,000 lb on the load.

worked.stem: A hydraulic jack has a 2 in² input piston and a 50 in² output piston. You push the input with 40 lb. What force lifts the load, and how far must the input piston travel to raise the load 1 in?
steps: Pressure: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 psi.
Pascal: the same 20 psi acts on the large piston, so force = 20 × 50 = 1,000 lb.
Area ratio = 50 ÷ 2 = 25, so the force is multiplied by 25.
Volume is conserved: 2 × d = 50 × 1, so d = 25 in. Force × 25, travel × 25: work in = work out.
worked.answer: 1,000 lb; the input piston moves 25 in

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Pressure is just force shared out per square inch. 40 lb on a 2 in² piston puts 40 ÷ 2 = 20 lb on each square inch.
Liquid can't be squashed, so it passes that 20 lb-per-square-inch push to every square inch it touches.
The big piston has 50 square inches. Each one gets 20 lb, so 50 × 20 = 1,000 lb in total.
Nothing is free. The liquid you push out of the thin cylinder spreads out thinly under the wide piston, so the big piston only rises a little.
The wide piston has 25 times the area, so it rises 1/25 as far. To lift it 1 in, you push the small piston 25 in.
Moving air works on pressure too: wherever the air speeds up, it presses less. A wing speeds the air over its top, so the top is pressed less than the bottom, and the wing is pushed up.

practice.stem: A 120 lb force is applied evenly over a 4 in² piston face. What pressure does it create?
practice.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 psi. 480 psi multiplies; 0.03 psi divides area by force.

practice.stem: A 20 lb force pushes the small piston of this hydraulic press. Ignoring friction, what force can the large piston exert on the load?
practice.explain: Pressure = 20 ÷ 3 lb/in², and the large piston gets that pressure over 45 in²: 20 × 45 ÷ 3 = 300 lb (area ratio 15). 1.3 lb flips the ratio; 900 lb multiplies by 45 without dividing by 3.

practice.stem: Water flows at 2 m/s through a pipe with a 0.06 m² cross-section into a section narrowed to 0.02 m². In the narrow section, the water flows at —
practice.explain: Continuity: 0.06 × 2 = 0.02 × v, so v = 6 m/s. By Bernoulli, faster flow means lower pressure. 0.67 m/s flips the area ratio.

practice.stem: In level flight, the average pressure under an aircraft's wings is 12 lb/ft² greater than the pressure on top. The total wing area is 180 ft². How much lift does this pressure difference produce?
practice.explain: Force = pressure × area = 12 × 180 = 2,160 lb of lift. 15 lb divides area by pressure; 216 lb is a place-value slip; 192 lb adds the numbers.

practice.stem: An aircraft produces 3,000 lb of lift at 100 knots. Keeping the same angle of attack and air density, how much lift does it produce at 150 knots?
practice.explain: Lift is proportional to airspeed squared: (150 ÷ 100)² = 1.5² = 2.25, and 3,000 × 2.25 = 6,750 lb. 4,500 lb assumes lift rises in direct proportion to speed; 10,125 lb cubes the ratio.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's picture pressure as a push on every single square inch.
steps: Pressure tells you the push on each square inch. 15 lb on a 1 in² piston is 15 lb on that one square inch: 15 psi.
Sealed liquid passes that same 15 psi to every square inch it touches.
A 20 in² piston has 20 square inches, each pushed with 15 lb: 300 lb in total.
The catch: the big piston moves only 1/20 as far as the small one, because the same volume of liquid spreads over 20 times the area.
Area depends on diameter squared: a piston twice as wide has 4 times the area.

In moving air or water, speeding up means pressing less. Squeeze a flow through a narrow throat and it speeds up and its pressure drops. Over a wing, the faster air on top presses less than the air underneath.

visual.caption: 15 psi on every square inch: 15 × 20 in² = 300 lb on the load.

example.stem: You push a 1 in² piston with 15 lb. The large piston is 20 in². What force acts on the load, and how far does the small piston move to raise the load 0.5 in?
steps: Pressure: 15 ÷ 1 = 15 psi.
Large piston: 15 × 20 = 300 lb.
Travel: 20 times the area means 20 times the distance on the small side: 0.5 × 20 = 10 in.
example.answer: 300 lb; the small piston moves 10 in

reteach.hook: Same pressure everywhere: more area, more force, less travel.

check.stem: A 25 lb force pushes the small piston. Ignoring friction, what force acts on the load?
check.explain: Pressure = 25 ÷ 2 = 12.5 psi. On 30 in²: 12.5 × 30 = 375 lb. 750 lb forgets to divide by the small piston's 2 in²; 1.7 lb flips the ratio.

check.stem: A hydraulic system's small piston is 1 in in diameter and its large piston is 4 in in diameter. A 50 lb force on the small piston produces what force on the large one?
check.explain: Area grows with diameter squared: (4 ÷ 1)² = 16 times the area, so 50 × 16 = 800 lb. 200 lb uses the diameter ratio (4) instead of the area ratio (16).

check.stem: A jack's large piston has 25 times the area of its small piston. To raise the load 2 in, how far must the small piston travel in total?
check.explain: The same volume of fluid moves both pistons, so the small one travels 25 times as far: 2 × 25 = 50 in. 0.08 in has the ratio upside down.

check.stem: Air enters a venturi tube (used to drive some aircraft gyro instruments) at 50 ft/s through a 12 in² opening and passes through a 3 in² throat. In the throat, the air —
options: moves at 200 ft/s with lower pressure than at the inlet
moves at 200 ft/s with higher pressure than at the inlet
moves at 12.5 ft/s with higher pressure than at the inlet
moves at 50 ft/s with the same pressure as at the inlet
check.explain: Continuity: 12 × 50 = 3 × v, so v = 200 ft/s. By Bernoulli, faster flow has lower pressure; that suction is what drives the instruments.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Pressure is how hard a force pushes on each bit of area.
Pressure = force ÷ area.
100 lb spread over 10 in² is 100 ÷ 10 = 10 lb on every square inch: 10 psi.
The same force on a smaller area makes a bigger pressure.
Push on liquid in a sealed tube and the same pressure is felt everywhere inside it.
A bigger piston has more square inches, so it gets more total force.
Moving air presses less on the surfaces beside it the faster it flows.
A wing makes air flow faster over its top, so the top is pushed less than the bottom. That difference is lift.

visual.caption: 10 lb on 1 in² is 10 psi. 10 psi on 10 in² is 100 lb.

example.stem: You press 10 lb on a 1 in² piston. The large piston has 10 in². What force pushes up the load?
steps: Pressure: 10 ÷ 1 = 10 psi.
The liquid passes 10 psi to the big piston.
10 psi × 10 in² = 100 lb.

reteach.hook: Pressure = force ÷ area. Bigger piston, bigger force.

check.stem: A 60 lb force presses evenly on 3 in². What is the pressure?
check.explain: Pressure = force ÷ area = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 psi. 180 psi multiplies; 0.05 psi divides the wrong way.

check.stem: The same 150 lb person stands first in flat boots, then on narrow heels. Which puts more pressure on the floor?
options: both the same, because the weight is the same
check.explain: Same force, much smaller area, so the narrow heels make far more pressure. Weight alone doesn't decide pressure; area matters.

check.stem: A 10 lb force pushes the small piston. Ignoring friction, what force acts on the load?
check.explain: 10 lb on 1 in² is 10 psi; 10 psi × 8 in² = 80 lb. 18 lb adds instead of multiplying.

check.stem: Air flows faster over the top of a wing than under it. The air pressure on top is therefore —
options: higher than underneath, pushing the wing down
lower than underneath, so the wing is pushed up
equal to underneath, because it is the same air
higher than underneath, pulling the wing up
check.explain: Faster-moving air has lower pressure (Bernoulli). Higher pressure underneath pushes the wing up: that is lift.
